History: long ago, when the elves were new to the world, they were split by discord, and the better-natured drove out those who were selfish and cruel. War between the two went on, the good elves always winning, until the dark ones were forced to leave the lands under the sky and seek safety underground. There, in lightless caverns and endless twisting passages hung with stone icicles, the dark elves, the drow, found refuge and comfort. Over the centuries they grew strong again and schooled themselves in the arcane arts. Though they became strong enough to face and perhaps defeat their former kin, they no longer wished to live in the sunlit world, content with the gloomy fairyland under the earth they had made their own. Yet they have neither forgiven nor forgotten, and above all else they hate their distant kin, elves and faeries, who drove them below and now live in the bright meadows and dells. They are seldom if ever seen by humans or demi-humans, but they still endure, sometimes coming up into lower dungeon levels and dealing with other creatures to further their schemes and take revenge on the dwellers of the upper world.

Levels: however many drow appear, one will always be of higher level than the rest.

  • Males are all at least 2nd-level fighters, some as high as 7th; males can also be magic-users, some as high as 12th level.
  • Females are also at least 2nd-level fighters, some up to 9th.
  • Most drow clerics are female, and no upper limit to their level is known; no male drow cleric is known above 4th level.

Arms and armour:

  • Armour: a fine, exquisitely made black mesh of steel alloyed with adamantite. Even the lowliest fighters have, in effect, +1 chainmail; higher-level drow have +2, +3, +4, or even +5. They also use small, oddly shaped bucklers; drow of higher level and importance have adamantite bucklers of +1, +2, or even +3. All drow move silently and with graceful speed even in their armour.
  • Weapons: a long dagger and short sword of adamantite alloy (+1, up to +3 or even +4 for nobles). 50% or more carry small one-handed crossbows (6” range, as a light crossbow) that shoot darts doing 1-3 points of damage and coated with a poison that knocks the victim unconscious (save at −4). A few carry adamantite maces (+1 to +5) and/or small javelins, poisoned like the darts, thrown with atlatls (9” range, +3/+2/+1 to hit at short/medium/long range).
  • Each drow carries a little personal wealth in a soft leather bag worn round the neck under the mail.

Abilities:

  • Superior infravision (12” range), and they move silently.
  • Boots and cloaks: their black boots and cloaks work like elven ones, except that the wearer has only a 75% chance of surprising enemies or blending into shadows. The material does not cut easily, and the cloaks give +6 on saving throws against fire, but any alteration to a cloak has a 75% chance of unravelling it and making it useless.
  • They are only 12½% (1 in 8) likely to be surprised.
  • Intelligent and highly co-ordinated, they can use either or both hands and arms to attack and defend.
  • Magic: they save at +2 against all magic spells (clerical included), from a caster or a device. Their magic resistance rises by 2% per level; multi-classed drow get this for only one class (the highest). So a 7th-level drow is 64% resistant to all magic and saves at +2 against any magic that could affect it.
  • Spells (once a day): all drow can use dancing lights, faerie fire, and darkness. Those above 4th level can also detect magic, know alignment, and levitate. Females can also use clairvoyance, detect lie, suggestion, and dispel magic.
  • They have dwarves’ powers concerning stone and things underground, and find hidden or secret doors as elves do.

Light: having lived so long in dark places, drow dislike bright light and will not go out in daylight except on the cloudiest, gloomiest days.

  • Within the radius of a light or continual light spell, they are 90% likely to be seen, lose 2 from dexterity, and attack at −2 to hit (targets get +2 on saving throws against their attacks where that applies).
  • Attacking targets inside such a radius, they are −1 to hit, and the targets get +1 on saves against their attacks.
  • In bright light, it is 75% likely they withdraw, unless that would endanger one of them, harm their aims, or expose something important to the intruders.
  • Dimmer light (torches, lanterns, magic weapons, fire beetle essence, or faerie fire) does not hinder them.

Languages: drow speak the underground trade language common to most intelligent underworld dwellers, common, gnome, elven, and their own language, plus others their intelligence allows; many know the languages of other underground races. All drow also have a highly sophisticated silent language of hand signs that can convey a great deal of complex information. Within 30’ of one another they also use facial expression, body movement, and posture, which alone convey a lot, and combined with hand and finger signs are as rich as any spoken language.

Ability scores:

  • Strength 8 + 1-6 (6 + 1-6 for males)
  • Intelligence 12 + 1-6 (10 + 1-8 for males)
  • Wisdom 8 + 1-10 (8 + 1-4 for males)
  • Dexterity 12 + 2-8
  • Constitution 4-16
  • Charisma 10 + 1-8 (8 + 1-8 for males)

Leaders by group size:

  • More than 10: also a male fighter/magic-user of at least 3rd level.
  • More than 20: also a female fighter/cleric of at least 6th clerical level, besides the male fighter/magic-user.
  • More than 30: 11-16 are females; the leader is a female cleric/fighter of at least 8th/7th level, the male fighter/magic-user is at least 5th/4th level, and each has an assistant of the level given earlier for those present with (the sentence ends here in the book).

Drow treasure: cloaks, armour, and weapons made by drow have special properties, though they do not radiate magic. They are made in the strange drow homeland, vast underground cities of carved stone and minerals, places of weird and fantastic beauty, flooded with unknown radiations that give the items their properties.

  • In direct sunlight they begin to decay irreversibly and become totally useless in 2-12 days.
  • Kept out of sunlight, they keep their properties for 31-50 days, then become normal items.
  • Exposed to the radiations of the drow homeland for 1 week in every 4, they could stay potent indefinitely.
  • Drow sleep poison decays instantly in sunlight and loses its effect 60 days after exposure to air in any case, though unopened packets stay potent for up to a year.

Description: drow have black skin and pale hair. They are slightly built, with long, delicate fingers and toes.
system.hpNote: Drow of higher level have hit dice by class and level (FF p.33).

system.description:
The enveloper is a mass of soft, shapeable flesh, roughly a cylinder 8’ tall and 3’ around. It can grow up to five limbs at will by reshaping its flesh, and in sight of humans or near-humans it takes a rough human shape (the limbs forming head, arms, and legs). It has animal intelligence, neutral alignment, standard magic resistance, and no psionic abilities.

  • Attacks: two “fists” for 1-8 hit points each.
  • Consuming: when it kills a victim, monster or character, it first falls on the body and consumes it completely in one melee round (it cannot attack that round), leaving clothes, weapons, etc. behind.
  • Gaining abilities: three melee rounds later (it can fight normally meanwhile), it can use any of the victim’s abilities: it gains the victim’s experience and knowledge, can speak with the victim’s voice, cast spells the victim had memorised, and so forth. It also gains 1-3 hit points per hit die of the victim, though it keeps attacking with the same chance to hit however many points it gains.
  • Many victims: each victim adds more abilities and powers. Where two conflict (in alignment, for example), one is discarded at random until the conflict is gone. It tends toward the alignment of its most recent victim, and its alignment language changes to match.
  • Growth: it gains hit dice with age, 2 dice at a time; in theory there is no limit to the hit dice or hit points an old enveloper may have.
system.hpNote: It gains hit dice in steps of 2 as it ages, and 1-3 hit points per hit die of each victim it consumes (FF p.34).

system.description:
The ettercap is a roughly man-sized biped with very long arms, a bulging pot-belly, short legs, and hairy skin. It has clawed hands and two poison fangs, one on each side of its mouth. Ettercaps are cruel, cunning, and treacherous, and get along well with every kind of spider.

  • Attacks: two claws for 1-3 hit points each and a poisonous bite for 1-8.
  • Silk: spider-like glands near the anus produce a thin, very tough silvery cord, which it makes into all sorts of weapons and devices: lariats, nets, garottes, tripwires, and so forth. Each ettercap has its favourite weapons and traps, so encounters vary, but given time it always lays traps and prepares an ambush.

At birth the eye killer is limbless and nearly round; later it grows a bat-like upper body on the body of a large snake. Its stunted wings cannot carry it. The upper body is dark grey-green and the lower part medium green flecked with dull yellow. Its eyes are disproportionately large and seem to be lidless.

It dislikes daylight and hates bright naked flame, living in dark places underground, where 2-8 may be found together (10% chance). How it behaves depends almost entirely on the light:

  • In darkness: against creatures relying only on infravision or dim natural light, it attacks only with its coils. A hit means it has wrapped a victim, doing 1-6 hit points of crushing damage, and every round after that it does 1-6 automatically, with no to-hit roll.
  • Death Stare: if a party carries lanterns or torches, it can use its dreaded Death Stare at up to 50’. Its eyes gather the light falling on them, amplify it enormously, and send it back at the light-bearer as a powerful, narrow ray. The ray strikes as if the victim were AC 10; he must save against death ray or die instantly, and takes 3-18 hit points even if he saves. If the stare is reflected, it does not harm the eye killer, which simply gathers the light, amplifies it further, and sends it at another victim in the same round. Fortunately, the Death Stare can be used only once per day.
  • Bright light close by: if torch- or lantern-bearers come close, it will not face the light, and tries to flee if it becomes intense (equal to three torches at 10’). If the light is not strong enough to drive it off, it attacks with its coils as above.

The eye of fear and flame is a hooded, man-sized figure whose face is always invisible; the inside of the hood looks like an opaque black screen. It constantly stalks the underworld looking for lawful or lawful/neutral parties or individuals, and commands an individual, or a member of a party, to do evil deeds. The deeds vary but are always evil. It has permanent know alignment and can speak all alignment languages, so it speaks to each person in the right alignment tongue. Only about twenty are rumoured to exist.

If attacked or disobeyed, it throws back its hood to reveal a bare skull with a red jewel in one eye socket and a black jewel in the other.

  • The red gem unleashes a 12-dice fireball once every three melee rounds.
  • The black gem acts as a wand of fear every melee round.
  • Each gem is worth 1,000-2,000 gold pieces, but they lose their properties when removed from the skull or when the creature is killed.
  • It has no way to fight hand-to-hand. If a fight goes against it, it shifts to the Ethereal Plane (taking two melee rounds) and tries to escape there.
  • Blindness or power word, blind cast on it is reflected back at the caster at full power.

It is said that these creatures were made either by the chaotic evil gods to destroy lawful beings, or by the lawful/neutral gods to test them. The truth is hidden.

Found only in rocky areas, this small dragonet (about 4’ long) looks like a miniature red dragon, if not in temper. If disturbed, even peacefully, there is a 50% chance it attacks. It is manoeuvrability class C in aerial combat.

  • Bite: 2-8 hit points; it does not use its claws in combat.
  • Breath: five times a day, a cone of fire 60’ long and 10’ across at the base, doing 2-16 hit points (half on a successful save). The breath is actually a jet of its blood.
  • Firedrakes live short lives compared to dragons, and the age-based hit point steps do not apply.

Blood: its blood burns fiercely in air, though it stays inert if kept in a container under water. A sword dipped in it becomes a flaming sword for 3-6 melee rounds, but each time a blow is struck during that time there is a cumulative 2% chance the sword breaks. If it survives, it returns to its normal powers when the flames die.

system.description:
Firenewts, sometimes called salamen, are distant relatives of lizard men. They live in sun-baked rocky hills, volcanic regions, or any other hot, dry, sometimes sulphurous place, above or below ground. They are cruel marauders, usually met as a hunting party, and delight in torturing and roasting victims alive before feasting on them.

Warriors and leaders:

  • Warriors (the most common kind) usually wear chainmail and carry normal weapons: pike and sword (45%), sword only (25%), pike and hand-axe (20%), or battle-axe (10%).
  • Elite warriors: one per ten warriors, with 3+3 hit dice and AC 3 (chain plus dexterity bonus). They always carry battle-axes.
  • Priests: per 30 firenewts, besides three elite warriors, there is one “priest” with 3+3 hit dice and AC 5, who uses a mace and has these druidic powers, each once per day: animal friendship, faerie fire, predict weather, produce flame, heat metal, and pyrotechnics.
  • Mounts: above ground, 33% of firenewts (90% of elite warriors, and all priests) ride giant striders. The priests train these beasts, which fight skilfully even if their rider dismounts.

Fire and cold:

  • Breath: once per turn, a firenewt can breathe fire on a foe directly in front of it within 5’, for 1-6 points of damage (half on a successful save).
  • They resist fire strongly, saving at +3 and taking 1 hit point less per attack die from fire.
  • Against cold they save at −3 and take 1 hit point more per attack die.

Lair: besides the warriors there are 70% more females, 150% young, and a secret, closely guarded hatching ground with 200% eggs. The priests control the hatching ground, which is guarded by 1-3 young fire lizards (see the MM, Lizard, Fire). The lair is ruled by an overlord firenewt of 4+4 hit dice and AC 3, with a close retinue of four elite warriors.

Description: a typical firenewt is mottled sepia, darkest along the spine and fading to near white on the belly. Its smooth flesh and features are eel-like, though its skin is dry, and its eyes deep crimson. Females are slightly shorter than males (about 5½’ tall) and a duller brown. The young are pale, darkening as they near maturity.

Fire snakes, coloured from blood-red to orange, are always found in fires: 1-6 in some large permanent fires, or one in smaller, semi-permanent fires such as fire pits and oil bowls. The gems they collect lie beneath them. It is thought that fire snakes are larval salamanders.

  • Surprise: they blend so well with their surroundings that they surprise 60% of the time.
  • Bite: 1-4 hit points, injecting a mild venom that paralyses the victim for 2-8 turns unless he saves against poison.

The firetoad is a large red toad about 4’ high, covered with warty purple growths. It shuns water and lives in dry regions above and below ground. It rarely (20% chance) attacks unless threatened, bothered, or defending its treasure.

  • Fireballs: its only attack is breathing small fireballs at will, with a range of 30’ and a blast radius of 5’, each doing damage equal to the firetoad’s remaining hit points. A normal saving throw halves the damage.
  • Water: throwing any liquid, even ordinary water, at it makes it retreat, but in the single melee round of its retreat it aims two fireballs at the person who threw it.

system.xp: 4HD: III/150 + 4 per hit point; 5HD: IV/205 + 5 per hit point; 6HD: V/350 + 6 per hit point
system.description:
This silicon-based mollusc averages 8’ high at the top of its shell. It has 4-6 club-like tentacles, kept in constant motion, flailing everything in its path. It is hypersensitive to bright light, so it is always met at night or underground.

  • Tentacles: each strikes for 1-8 hit points and has its own hit points; a “dead” tentacle stops attacking. Each tentacle counts as 1 HD, so a snail with 5 tentacles has 5 hit dice.
  • Body: it pulls its body into its shell so fast that the body counts as AC −8, but any hit on the body kills it outright, even if some tentacles survive.
  • Death throes: once all tentacles are killed, it withdraws into its shell and dies in 1-3 turns, giving pitiful wailing cries with a 50% chance per turn of attracting a wandering monster.
  • Immunities: fire (normal or magical) and poison.
  • Shell and magic: its brightly coloured shell protects it partly against magic, like a robe of scintillating colours. A spell aimed at it has a 40% chance of malfunctioning, 30% of working normally, 20% of not working at all, and 10% of being reflected onto the caster. A malfunctioning spell’s effects change (entirely at the referee’s discretion, but only slightly) and the changed effect is deflected from the snail to the nearest person or creature.

The shell weighs 250 pounds (2,500 gold pieces weight), keeps its magical properties for 1-6 months after the snail dies, and can be sold for as much as 5,000 gold pieces.
system.hpNote: Each tentacle is 1 hit die with its own hit points; any hit on the body (AC −8) kills the snail outright (FF p.38).

system.description:
Flinds are powerful humanoid relatives of gnolls, 6½’ tall, who always attack at +1 to hit because of their strength. Most of their traits and habits are like gnolls’ (see the MM), and gnolls regard them as higher beings (a flind’s charisma is at least 16 in a gnoll’s eyes). A large group of gnolls is sometimes led by one or more flinds.

  • Club: the normal flind usually fights with a club for 1-6 hit points.
  • Flindbar: 25% of a group carry instead a pair of chain-linked iron bars, which they move so fast they get two attacks per round. Either attack that hits does 1-4 hit points, and the victim must also save (as against wands) or his weapon is tangled in the chains and he is disarmed. Any character with both strength and dexterity of 13 or better can use a flindbar, provided he practises with it and takes it as a weapon of proficiency.
  • Leaders: one per 15 flinds. They have 3+3 hit dice, 17 strength, and high intelligence, with 18 charisma as far as gnolls are concerned. All leaders use flindbars in melee.

Flinds speak the same languages as gnolls and are friendly with orcs, hobgoblins, bugbears, and ogres, but dislike trolls and will not co-operate with them.

These strange, saucer-shaped creatures are pure white. The mouth is in the middle of the upper surface, which is AC 0, with a 4” eyestalk on each side of it. The underside is AC 8 and bears a mass of small spikes and many small tentacles.

  • Flight: it “flies” by sucking air into its mouth and blowing it out through its underside. It normally floats about 4’ above the ground but can rise up to 10’, especially to attack. It is manoeuvrability class D.
  • Squirt: it normally drives off attackers with a squirt of foul-smelling liquid from an opening on its “equator” (its widest horizontal line), striking anyone within a 60° arc up to 20’. A victim who fails a save versus poison flees in disgust, and for 1-4 hours his companions cannot bear to have him within 100’.
  • Drop attack: if that fails, it rises above a chosen victim and drops straight down on him. The spikes do 1-8 hit points in all, and the tentacles fill the wounds with acid doing another 1-4, repeating for the next 2-8 rounds unless magic is used to neutralise it (alchemists have so far failed to make an antidote).
  • A flumph turned over is helpless.

It can speak the lawful alignment tongues, though with a very limited vocabulary.

Forlarren are descended from the offspring of a good nymph and the greater devil who enslaved her. They hate their own limbo-like existence and wander alone, seeking vengeance on good and evil alike. They speak a crude form of the common tongue.

  • Fists: they attack characters on sight, using their fists as cudgels for 1-4 points each.
  • Heat metal: once a day, by contact, a forlarren can heat metal, and uses it on the first opponent in metal armour it meets in melee. All targets count as AC 10 for this attack. If it hits, the victim takes 3-18 hit points each round contact lasts if wearing plate mail, or 2-16 per round in lighter metal armour (including all magical metal armour). Once made, contact lasts until the forlarren or its victim is dead. A successful save (versus dragon breath) halves the damage.
  • Remorse: as soon as it has killed one character, its divided nature shows. It is overcome with remorse and offers the survivors its services and powers (the blood of its ancestral mother still runs in its veins). After a while its dominant evil side takes over again, and it leaves the party. From then on it attacks on sight again, including the party it befriended if it meets them again.
  • How long: the friendship cannot be predicted exactly. As a guide the referee may choose 1-6 days, with a 10% chance of it being shorter (13-24 hours) or longer (7-10 days).

Native tribes greatly fear frost men because of their deadly talent and call them “ice demons”, though in most ways they are like normal humans. They look like ordinary human men, dress in loose animal skins, and carry their personal treasure in leather sacks. They radiate cold, easily felt from as far as 30’, though not strong enough to do damage.

  • Classes: they can have the abilities of fighters, clerics, thieves, or even magic-users, and carry weapons to match. On the little evidence available, most (75%) are fighters, 15% thieves, about 8% clerics, and only 2% magic-users. Their clerics and magic-users seem to have developed spell use only to the equivalent of 2nd experience level.
  • Ice mist: three times a day, a frost man can send a freezing cone of ice mist, 35’ long and 10’ across at the base, from one eye (usually kept under a patch). Everyone in the cone takes 3-18 hit points (half on a save versus dragon breath). His other eye focuses normally, so he has no to-hit penalty for using one eye.

So far they have only been met singly, and their lairs and way of life are unknown. It is thought there are villages of frost men, with women and children, hidden in deep mountain caves, mainly in cold regions, but no one has yet gone to find out.

The galltrit is a small (½’ tall) winged gremlin with a nasty temper, found in places with dung, carrion, or offal. It is stone grey, which with its small size makes it hard to notice: humans and most demi-humans detect one on 1 in 8, elves on 1 in 6. It is manoeuvrability class B in aerial combat.

  • Attack: if disturbed (by noise, for example), it flies onto a victim, preferably unnoticed, and bites for 1-2 hit points, locking its teeth into the skin. If it gains surprise, this first attack is +3 to hit.
  • Blood drain: its saliva numbs the skin around the bite for a full turn, while it sucks blood for 1 hit point per melee round. An anti-coagulant in the saliva also lowers the victim’s constitution by one point every four melee rounds, for as many days as hit points drained. For example, after 10 melee rounds it has drained 10 points of blood and the victim has lost two points of constitution, restored after 10 days.
  • Going unnoticed: it rarely stays on a victim for more than one full turn, even if unnoticed, and tries to flee as soon as it is detected. If its first bite is not noticed, the numbness means the victim will not notice it afterwards either; only after a while, when he senses the blood loss and his weakening constitution, will he think to look for the cause.
  • Collapse: a victim who loses three constitution points (even temporarily) collapses, which almost certainly reveals the galltrit. He takes two full turns to recover, and 12 days to regain the lost constitution.

These extraordinary creatures are man-sized, with a powerful human torso and two arms ending in very sharp claws. On a thin but very strong neck sits a skull, usually an animal’s but sometimes a primitive man’s. The lower body is a cylinder of muscle and skin that can be compressed and released like a spring, with three long, thin, single-toed feet below. Having no legs as such, it moves in a series of springs: jumping straight up, its head can just reach a 14’ ceiling, and moving forward it is as fast as a 12” movement rate.

Ambush: it normally waits upright in its lair, a pit about 6’ deep, with its head just at ground level. It shores up the sides of the pit and makes a cover of rock, wood, rags, and old bones, so that an approaching adventurer sees no pit, only a skull apparently lying on the ground. If a living creature comes within 2’ of the pit’s edge (about 4’ from the skull), it springs out and attacks.

  • First it attacks with its bite only, for 1-8 hit points; after that with its bite and two claws (1-4 hit points each).
  • If the fight goes against it, it flees rather than fight to the death.

Treasure: from its victims it takes only coins, gems, and small pieces of jewellery, storing them on the floor of its pit or in a cache hole in the pit wall, packed tightly with earth.

Though solitary, gambados often dig their pits near others of their kind; where bones are plentiful, as many as 8 may have pits close together, though they do not seem to communicate with each other.

Both kinds of garbug look like lobsters with wasp bodies. They can fly, rather clumsily, on flimsy wings, but usually walk on their six legs. They are manoeuvrability class D in aerial combat.

  • Tentacles: six tentacles, each 2’ long, surround the mouth and flail at prey. They do no damage as such, but ooze a paralysing secretion (save versus paralysation or be paralysed).
  • In melee, each kind attacks with its tentacles plus its own “specialist” weapon.

Black garbug: a uniform glossy black. Besides its tentacles it has a proboscis that strikes at a victim within 5’, doing 1-4 hit points on a hit, at the same time as its tentacles flail.

Violet garbug: unlike its black cousin it has no proboscis. Instead, as well as its tentacles, it attacks with two large pincers placed like a lobster’s, each doing 1-6 hit points. It is a uniform, striking violet except for its claws, which are deep yellow.

system.specialAttacks: Hurling rocks for 2-20 points of damage
system.description:
Fog giants are cousins of cloud giants. On the very rare occasions when as many as six are met, a cloud giant is always with them. They live in foggy places such as marshes, swamps, dense forests, and sea coasts.

  • Senses and surprise: their very keen hearing and highly developed sense of smell mean they are surprised only on a 1 (d6). They can also blend into fog, surprising opponents 80% of the time.
  • Fighting: they love massive ornate swords and fight with them or with their fists, doing 4-24 hit points either way. They prefer armour of white dragon hide studded with silver, but armour does not change their AC, which is always 1.
  • Rocks: adults, like cloud giants, can hurl rocks from 1” to 24”, doing 2-20 hit points on a hit, and have a 45% chance of catching similar missiles.

They have milk-white skin, silvery white hair, and black, piercing eyes. They speak their alignment language and their own dialect of the giant tongue, which only cloud giants among other giants can understand.

Giants: general (FF)

Giants are huge humanoids. Besides the six major races of giants (see the MM, Giant), there are at least these two sub-races. Their shared traits are given here; what is unique to each is under its own heading.

  • Strength: all giants are very strong, with strength from 21 to 30 on the human scale. This lets them pick up rocks and hurl them as if shot from a catapult, but without a catapult’s minimum range.
  • Sacks: whenever they leave their lair, giants of every kind carry a huge sack holding odds and ends precious only to the giant: a large rock or two, and 1,000 to 6,000 coins of some kind, usually gold.
  • Dealings: giants are often stupid but usually cunning too. They can sometimes be tricked, and are likely to bargain if approached from a position of strength. Eager for treasure, they will often join an undertaking with creatures of similar alignment.
  • Young giants have hit points and do damage according to the percentage of a normal adult male shown by the dice roll.
  • Languages: each race speaks its own dialect, which other races cannot understand, plus its alignment tongue.

system.specialAttacks: Hurling rocks for 2-16 points of damage
system.description:
Mountain giants are rarely met outside their lair, a huge cavern carved out of the heart of a rocky mountain. Besides their own tongue, all of them speak the ogre language. They have light tan to light reddish-brown skin and, like hill giants, dress in rough hides or skins.

  • Rocks: like hill giants, they can hurl rocks from 1” to 20”, doing 2-16 hit points on a hit, and catch similar missiles 30% of the time.
  • Melee: huge clubs, doing 4-40 hit points.
  • Servants: a mountain giant can summon and control other monsters: usually (70%) 6-15 ogres, sometimes (20%) 4-9 trolls, or even (10%) 1-4 hill giants. In its lair, it is 75% likely these creatures are there as servants and guards.
  • Families: giantesses and young are rarely met. If four mountain giants are met in their lair, there is also one female and one young giant (each with hit dice of 8+1-2 and 1 attack for 2-16 hit points); otherwise all mountain giants met are adult males.
