  • Strength: all giants are very strong, with strength from 21 to 30 on the human scale. This lets them pick up rocks and hurl them as if shot from a catapult, but without a catapult’s minimum range.
  • Sacks: whenever they leave their lair, giants of every kind carry a huge sack holding odds and ends precious only to the giant: a large rock or two, and 1,000 to 6,000 coins of some kind, usually gold.
  • Dealings: giants are often stupid but usually cunning too. They can sometimes be tricked, and are likely to bargain if approached from a position of strength. Eager for treasure, they will often join an undertaking with creatures of similar alignment.
  • Young giants have hit points and do damage according to the percentage of a normal adult male shown by the dice roll.
  • Languages: each race speaks its own dialect, which other races cannot understand, plus its alignment tongue.

system.magicResistance: Standard but +2 bonus on saving roll and immune to magical fire
system.description:
These large, flightless, featherless birds look like heavy ostriches. Firenewts use them as steeds. They are generally fearless and never check morale.

  • Fireballs: beside each of its two dully glowing red eyes is a small duct that can shoot a small fireball doing 1-6 hit points. It can fire two per hour (one from each duct), with the accuracy of a +4 longbow, a maximum range of 50’, and a burst radius of 10’.
  • Bite or kick: it can bite to the front or flank for 1-8 hit points, or kick to the rear for 1-10, but cannot do both in the same melee round, and usually attacks toward wherever it was last hit.
  • Fire: immune to all fire, magical or not. In fact its body draws nourishment from heat, so it is most at home in deserts and volcanic regions. Intense heat, flames, fireballs, and the like act as a cure light wounds spell on it once every three rounds, so giant striders are often seen wading in lava beds or standing in the flames of a forest fire (the phoenix legend may have come from such a sight).
  • Cold and water: cold spells and the like do 2-7 extra hit points, and water is poison to it if drunk. Even cold liquid thrown over it does some damage (at the referee’s discretion, normally 1-2 hit points).

Gibberlings are pale, hunched, naked humanoids with short legs and long arms, usually found in desolate woods or dark caverns underground. The underground kind loathe bright light and are especially afraid of fire.

  • Attack: they attack in huge numbers, howling and chattering insanely. The noise makes even the boldest hirelings check morale each round, though player characters are unaffected.
  • Weapons: normal swords, which they use so skilfully they get +1 to hit.
  • They always fight to the death, relying on sheer numbers to overwhelm their enemies, which means almost any creature that dares enter their territory, for they are highly aggressive.

They clearly have some primitive way of communicating among themselves, but no language anyone can discern. Oddly, for creatures that attack in such numbers, no leaders have ever been found among them, nor apparently any gibberlings of a class other than fighter.

History: thousands of years ago the mind flayers (see the MM, Mind Flayer) conquered a race of evil humans and bound them to service, usually as slaves, sometimes picking choice victims to eat. For centuries the humans resented this but lacked the strength to throw off the yoke. Slowly and secretly they built up their powers, until under their supreme leader Gith they rebelled and, after a long and vicious struggle, won their freedom. From then on they were called githyanki, and quickly became known as powerful psionicists and deadly fighters with an instinct for violence.

Where they live: they now live on the Astral Plane, in huge castles, but from time to time project themselves to the Prime Material Plane (an innate ability of the whole race) and set up temporary underground refuges as bases for raids on humans and mind flayers alike. If they meet humans and mind flayers together, they destroy the mind flayers first and may seem to be co-operating with the humans, but once the mind flayers are dead they turn on the humans too. They move at 96” on the Astral Plane.

Religion: they worship a lich-queen said to have powers at the 24th level of magic use or higher.

Classes: fighters, magic-users, or fighter/magic-users. They have no rangers, monks, druids, or assassins, though illusionists are sometimes (5%) met, and they have a kind of anti-paladin, the knight. None has ever been known to rise above 11th level, and they rarely pass 9th; it is assumed the lich-queen destroys any who become strong enough to threaten her.

Castles: each is ruled by a supreme leader, a fighter/magic-user of 10th/8th or 11th/9th level, with power of life and death over all beneath him. Each castle also holds 40 knights (9th-level anti-paladins), the supreme leader’s elite force and personal guard, and up to 1,000 githyanki of lower rank.

Arms and armour: they use armour and weapons as men do, often distinguished by their ornate design.

  • On war expeditions they wear +4 splint mail (AC 0) and carry no shields.
  • Fighters and fighter/magic-users of 5th level and above usually (50% chance) carry +1 two-handed swords, otherwise normal ones.
  • Fighters of 7th level and above usually (60%) carry a +2 or +3 longsword.
  • Knights of 7th level and above always (100%) have a silver sword: a +3 two-handed sword that, used astrally, has a 20% chance per melee round of cutting the silver cord (this does not affect victims with a mind bar).
  • A supreme leader wields a special silver sword that is +5, fully vorpal, and affects victims with a mind bar.
  • Silver swords are unaligned but have intelligence of 8 or more and suitable powers. The githyanki will go to almost any length to keep one out of human hands; losing a special silver sword immediately brings a very powerful raiding party to recover it, whose members die instantly if they fail.

Parties: outside their Prime Material Plane lairs they are rarely met in parties of more than 4: typically two trainees of any of the three classes (levels 1-3), one fighter of level 4-6, and a leader fighter/magic-user of 7th/6th level. Rarely (10%) a party is on a special mission; it then has only one trainee and is led by an 8th-level knight.

Lairs: a lair houses 21-30 githyanki, typically:

1 supreme leader11th level fighter or 7th/8th level fighter/magic-user
2 captains8th level fighter and 7th/6th level fighter/magic-user
1 knight8th level anti-paladin
2 warlocksmagic-users of 4th-7th level
3 sergeantsfighters of 4th-7th level
2 “gish”fighter/magic-users of 4th/4th level
10-19 lower levelsevenly distributed between the three possible classes, with experience levels 1st-3rd

Large parties: very occasionally (5% chance) a party of more than four is met, on a particularly purposeful mission (not hunting a lost silver sword, which brings out an even larger and stronger party). Expect 5-10 individuals, led by the lair’s supreme leader with one of the captains, the knight, and 2-7 “lower ranks” evenly distributed. In a lair or a large party there is a 5% chance of a 6th-level illusionist in place of one of the lower-level members.

Magic items: normal human chances for items other than swords. A Prime Material Plane lair holds 5-10 magic items chosen to suit the mission. A small party usually (75%) has one magic item; a larger party 1-10.

Red dragons: the githyanki have a pact with a group of red dragons (see the MM, Dragon, Red), which, in return for shelter, food, and treasure, carry them as steeds on the Prime Material Plane. A dragon (above sub-adult) carries 4-6 githyanki for its size plus 1-5 for its age: a small young adult dragon carries 5 (4 for size, 1 for age), an average-sized old dragon 8 (5 for size, 3 for age), and a huge ancient dragon 11 (6 for size, 5 for age). On the Prime Material Plane these dragons obey only githyanki.
system.hpNote: Hit dice follow class and level (never above 11th level); roll them as for a character of that class (FF p.43).

system.description:
The githzerai live in limbo, alongside the slaadi, and roam the Prime Material Plane like the githyanki, with whom they are constantly at war. Oddly, both are offshoots of the race freed from mind flayer bondage by Gith, yet the war is vicious and long-lasting. Githzerai are generally slightly weaker than githyanki, but their magic resistance seems to make up for it, and neither side stays on top for long. With the mind flayers they keep an uneasy truce, constantly broken by isolated skirmishes.

Classes: the same limits as the githyanki, except that some githzerai specialise as monks, and they have nothing like the githyanki anti-paladin. They fight with silver swords and other weapons as githyanki do, with the same chances of having a particular item, but seem not to have developed the special silver swords. Their political organisation is the same; they are ruled by an undying wizard-king said to be of 16th/23rd level of fighting/magic use, who keeps githzerai from rising beyond 9th level.

Style: where githyanki favour baroque armour, ornate weapons, and showy magic, githzerai are monastic: their weapons very plain, their magic economical in movement and direct in effect.

Fortresses: they hold a few fortresses on the Prime Material Plane, very strong holdings with adamantite walls rising like huge squat towers from dusty plains. Each houses about 500 githzerai.

Psionics: all githzerai have astral projection, mind bar, probability travel, and energy control at 6th level of mastery. Their psionic powers are highly developed, with all attack/defence modes.

Parties: outside their lair they are rarely met in parties of more than 4: typically two trainees of any of the three main classes (fighter, magic-user, or fighter/magic-user, levels 1-2), one fighter of level 3-5, and a leader fighter/magic-user of 5th/5th level. There is only a 5% chance of a character with monkish abilities, but if there is one, he is of 6th-8th level, since monks are mainly trained in the fortresses.

Lairs: a lair is a temporary base for hunting and war and houses 21-30 githzerai, roughly:

1 supreme leader9th level fighter or 4th/7th level fighter/magic-user
1 captain6th level fighter or 5th/5th level fighter/magic-user
2 warlocksmagic-users of 3rd-5th level
3 sergeantsfighters of 3rd-6th level
3 “zerths”fighter/magic-users of 3rd/3rd level
11-201st-2nd levels, evenly distributed between the three possible classes

If a monk is present (10% chance), he replaces one of the lower-level githzerai and is of 6th-8th level.

Magic items: normal human chances (except for swords). A lair holds 2-16 magic items.

Large parties are organised much like large githyanki parties, depending partly on how important the mission is. A typical one has the supreme leader, both warlocks, 2 of the sergeants, a zerth, and 4-7 of 1st or 2nd level. If the lair has a monk, he always goes with a large party.
system.hpNote: Hit dice follow class and level (never above 9th level); roll them as for a character of that class (FF p.45).

system.description: The goldbug is a beetle with a flat, round, golden shell the size and shape of a gold piece. It is very sluggish and spends most of its time asleep, often on a pile of gold coins; only very close examination tells it apart from the coins. So, though it has no treasure of its own, it lives in other creatures’ treasure. When disturbed it bites like a large spider: 1-4 hit points, and the victim must save versus poison or die.

The gorbel is an odd creature: a red globe of thin, rubbery material about 3’ across, with a tiny mouth, six tiny eyes on short retractable stalks spaced around its upper half, and two clawed legs on which it moves remarkably fast. Its good armour class comes from its high dexterity. Gorbels are mischievous, fickle, and irritable, and usually attack.

  • Attack: it tries to clamp itself onto a victim’s back with its claws, attacking at first as a 2 HD creature. A hit means it has done so, doing 1-4 hit points. After that it cannot be removed until dead, and automatically claws its victim each round for 1-6 points.
  • Once attached, it loses its dexterity bonus and its AC becomes 10.
  • Weapons: blunt weapons do not harm it, but a hit with a pointed or edged weapon bursts it, killing it and doing 1-4 hit points of blast damage to everyone within 5’.
system.hpNote: No hit points are given: any hit with a pointed or edged weapon bursts it, and blunt weapons do not harm it (FF p.46).

system.specialAttacks: Hugs for 2-12 hit points of damage
system.description:
Gorilla bears have a gorilla’s head, body, and legs with a bear’s sharp teeth and powerful arms. They have the aggressive temper of the grizzly and the meat-eating habits of the cave bear. Excellent hearing, smell, and eyesight mean they are rarely (15%) surprised, and their high dexterity improves their AC.

  • Paws: two, for 1-8 hit points each.
  • Hug: a paw hit with a roll of 18 or better also means a hug for 2-12 more hit points. If 18 would not hit the victim, the hug happens only on a roll of 19, or if that would not hit either, on a 20. A 20 always means a hug, whatever the victim’s AC.
  • Unlike a normal bear, it cannot keep fighting once its hit points drop below zero.

The grell is a fearsome sight: a body like a giant exposed brain about 5’ across, with a beak at the front and ten 6’ long tentacles trailing beneath. It “flies” by levitation, steering with small movements of its tentacles, and is manoeuvrability class D. Grell are usually found underground, sometimes in ruined or abandoned buildings. They are especially dangerous and vicious, dropping on victims from above whenever they can.

  • Tentacles: all ten attack a single victim. Each does 1-4 hit points, and small spines on it inject venom that paralyses the victim unless he saves against paralysation at +4.
  • Once a victim is paralysed by any tentacle, each round after that two tentacles stay anchored to him while the other eight lash him (1-4 hit points each) and the beak tears him (1-6 hit points). None of these attacks after the first paralysis needs a to-hit roll; lucky is he who escapes alive once a grell has him.
  • Damaging it: any hit on a tentacle disables it (it regrows in 1-2 days if the grell survives), but that damage does not come off the grell’s hit points; only hits on the body hurt it in the usual way. Body and tentacles are all AC 4.
  • It is immune to lightning, with standard resistance to other normal and magical attacks.

The body is drab olive streaked with white; the tentacles are pale olive-green.

system.magicResistance: Save as 6th level fighter (and see below)
system.treasure: Individuals K, L, M; in lair B
system.xp: Warriors: II/28 + 2 per hit point; Leaders: II/50 + 3 per hit point; Champions: III/85 + 4 per hit point
system.description:
Grimlocks are fierce humanoid warriors of deep caverns, who come up only in raiding parties, roaming the surface late at night to find humans to butcher and eat. They are powerfully built, with thick, scaly grey skin, long, black, usually unkempt hair, and white, very sharp teeth, and are usually dressed in dark rags.

  • Senses: their eyes are blank and sightless, but their very keen hearing and smell give them effective “vision” within 20’. They are immune to spells that work on sight, such as phantasmal force, darkness, invisibility, and mirror image. However, audible glamer and the like partly “blind” them, cutting their “vision” to 10’ and their chance to hit by 2; inhaling snuff and similar substances does the same.
  • Camouflage: in rocky terrain they blend with their surroundings; while motionless they cannot be detected except by detect invisibility (unless someone actually bumps into them).
  • Saves: all grimlocks, warrior, leader, or champion, save as 6th-level fighters.

Weapons: they prefer edged, blood-letting weapons. They can fight bare-handed (1-6 hit points), but are usually (90%) armed as follows:

WeaponChance
hand-axe20%
battle-axe15%
two-handed sword15%
bastard sword15%
broad sword15%
long sword20%

Leaders and champions wield a battle-axe or two-handed sword.

Leaders and lairs: for every 10 grimlocks there is a “leader” of 3 hit dice and AC 4, and for every 40 also a “champion” of 4 hit dice and AC 3. A lair also has females (80% as many as the males, each 1 hit die, AC 6) and young (as many as the males, each 1 hit point, AC 6, non-combatant).

Allies: grimlocks rarely mix with other beings, though there is a small (10%) chance they let medusae share their lair, and a 2% chance a wandering group has 1-2 mind flayers with it. For that last reason githyanki particularly hate them.

system.xp: 2HD: II/28 + 2 per hit point; 3HD: II/50 + 3 per hit point; 4HD: III/85 + 4 per hit point
system.description:
The gryph is an eagle-sized bird with many legs, usually four, though some with six or even eight have been seen. It has a razor-sharp beak and powerful jaws, and usually attacks at high speed from high in the shadows of an underground cavern. Its bite does 2-12 hit points. It is manoeuvrability class B in aerial combat.

Egg-laying: if 3 or more are met, one is female, with a 35% chance she is ready to lay. Such a female tries to grapple a victim with her legs instead of biting; if she hits, she injects her tiny eggs into the bloodstream through a thin tube from her abdomen. This does no damage.

  • Surviving eggs hatch in 1-3 days, killing the victim at once and releasing 1-4 baby gryphs. (Far more eggs are injected; 1-4 is the number that survive the 1-3 days.)
  • Meanwhile the victim feels slight discomfort and abdominal swelling, growing to agony just before hatching.
  • Before hatching, cure disease or dispel evil cast on the victim kills the eggs; so will a wish or similar spell, properly used.

These daemons vary in size and form; examples met have looked like type II or type IV demons, large bears, and wild cats. Evil high priests summon them to guard treasure. Their movement in melee is 9”, but they are bound never to leave the treasure they guard unless their summoner releases them.

Whatever their shape, they always share these traits:

  • immunity to charm, hold, sleep, polymorph, and fear;
  • immunity to non-magical weapons and to magical weapons of less than +2;
  • the ability to speak and understand all languages;
  • fire breath in a cone 30” long and 10” across at the base, doing 5-30 hit points (half on a save).

They cannot use their breath on a target within 10’, so in melee they bite (1-6 hit points) and use two claws (1-12 hit points each). The way they are summoned usually (80%) also makes them invulnerable to one other particular form of attack (fire or swords, for example).

They have no treasure of their own on the Prime Material Plane (they may well own some in their home), and are always guarding their summoner’s treasure, so determine treasure by the summoner. It usually includes at least one clerical scroll and/or clerical magic device.

The guardian familiar takes the form of a small black cat set by a high-level wizard to guard treasure, so it may be of any alignment (its summoner’s). It never leaves its place on top of the treasure or chest, and attacks only if attacked itself or if someone tries to get at the treasure.

  • Attacks: two raking claws (1-4 hit points each) and a bite (1-6 hit points). As it fights it grows steadily bigger, until it looks like a bobcat, shrinking back to normal if the fight stops; this seems meant to frighten robbers.
  • Magic resistance: depends on its master’s level: 50% for a 10th-level magic-user’s familiar, changing by 5% per level either way (30% for a 6th-level master, 75% for a 15th-level master). A magic-user of 4th level or below cannot get one.
  • If attackers break off at any time, it does not pursue but returns to its duty.

Nine lives: it is the source of the legend of the cat with nine lives. Each time it is killed, up to the 9th time, it is instantly reborn stronger: add 1 hit die (re-roll hit points), add 2” to its movement, improve its AC by 1, and add 1 point of damage to each attack. So after being killed four times it is reborn at “5th level”, with AC 4, a movement rate of 20”, 5 hit dice, and attacks for 5-8/5-8/5-10. Killed a ninth time, it stays dead.

  • This build-up can be stopped by disintegrate, flesh to stone, temporal stasis, and of course wish and alter reality (properly used), or powers that copy them, as long as its magic resistance is overcome.
  • Holy (unholy) word banishes it to its home plane.

Do not confuse it with the ordinary familiar of the 1st-level magic-user spell find familiar (see the PHB, Character Spells). The means of summoning a guardian familiar involve casting find familiar, but are known only to a small group of arcane magicians (and the few they train in their specialist art), and are believed to involve bargaining with the beings of the Outer Planes where the guardian familiars live.
system.hpNote: Each time it is slain (up to the 9th time) it is reborn with 1 more hit die: re-roll its hit points (FF p.49).

system.magicResistance: 20% and immune to charm, sleep and similar spells
system.description:
Hellcats are the companions and familiars of devils and are usually found on their home levels of Hell. Now and then one journeys to the Prime Material Plane to serve Hell’s ends by becoming the servant of a powerful lawful evil character.

Appearance: it is invisible in the presence of any light. In darkness it can be seen as a faintly glowing, wraith-like outline with blazing crimson eyes, shaped like a house cat the size of a tiger.

  • Attacks: two claws for 2-5 hit points each and a bite for 2-12.
  • Defences: only magical weapons can harm it, and even then their magical damage bonuses do not count (a +2 dagger does 1-4 hit points rather than 3-6, for example). It has a base 20% magic resistance and is completely immune to all mind-controlling spells (charm, hold, sleep, suggestion, etc.).

Choosing a master: a hellcat not already attached to anyone picks the most powerful lawful evil member of a party and serves him. Among equally high-level lawful evil members it prefers a cleric, then a magic-user or illusionist, then a fighter, then other classes. It serves only intelligent lawful evil creatures. Once it has a master it serves him in evil deeds, protects and defends him, and communicates only with him, by telepathy with a range of 9”.

Its price: its only demand is one living human victim per week to eat. The master must provide it; if he fails, he becomes the meal himself.

Breaking the bond:

  • A hellcat always leaves its master for a new, more powerful lawful evil master whenever it meets one, provided the new master will have it (if not, the old bond stays). If the new master accepts it, it has no qualms about attacking its former master on command. So a character may “steal” a hellcat from one monster only to have it “stolen” from him by another.
  • It can serve on the Prime Material Plane for only a year and a day, then must return home to Hell. It may come back later, but its bond with its old master is not automatically restored; if the master meets it again, he may gain its service the same way as before.

Meeting one:

  • A hellcat already serving someone may switch allegiance as above, or stay with its master.
  • If no one in the party is lawful evil: it flees if the party includes anyone neutral evil or chaotic evil, and attacks if no one in the party is evil in any combination.

Hoar foxes live in cold regions, usually in small packs, and are rarely (10% chance) aggressive unless threatened. But their beautiful silver-grey pelts are valuable (an undamaged one fetches 100 gold pieces on the open market), so adventurers often threaten them.

  • Bite: 1-6 hit points.
  • Breath: their main weapon is a cone of cold with a range of 30”, wide enough to catch only one victim, doing 2-12 hit points (half on a save). For this attack the victim counts as AC 10, though dexterity adjustments are allowed.
  • Fire and cold: immune to cold attacks, but they take double damage from fire (which also, of course, ruins the pelt).

Hook horrors are large, powerful bipeds with vulture-like heads and a hard, plated, mottled grey shell. They live in deep underground corridors and chambers. Their sight is very poor but their hearing extremely keen, so there is only a 10% chance of surprising one. Their arms end in sharp, hooked talons, each doing 1-8 hit points in melee. They cannot speak, but talk to each other by clacking their shells, an eerie sound that can alarm the unwary as it echoes through dungeon corridors.

This very aggressive insect has a body 5’ long and a wingspan of 10’ or more. It is manoeuvrability class B in aerial combat. Its natural home is coniferous forest, though one is sometimes met underground.

Sting: it attacks on sight. A hit has these effects:

  • 1-4 hit points of damage;
  • 5-30 points of poison damage (a save negates);
  • incapacity for 2-12 hours (a save also negates).

Roll one saving throw for the poison and one for the incapacity.

  • Smoke and flame hamper it, making it strike at −2 and −4 to hit respectively.
  • Warning: fortunately for its victims, its loud buzz can be heard 150’ away in dungeon corridors (halved for each door in between, up to three doors).

One of the legendary beasts whose appearance is said to foretell death, it looks like a dark, shadowy wolfhound 5’ tall at the shoulder. It is rumoured that only one exists. It is said to appear only when a character has seriously offended his deity, for example by a flagrant act against his alignment.

  • Sighting: it appears instantly and stays in view only a few seconds, visible to just one member of a party. Because its appearance is so brief and its form so shadowy, it cannot be harmed in any way.
  • Howl: the one who sees it hears it give a booming howl before it vanishes. There is no saving throw. The next 1-10 wounds the victim suffers do quadruple damage, and until he has taken that many wounds no healing (cure wounds spells, for instance) works on him. If he survives them, the howl has no further effect.
  • Remove curse: cast on the victim within one turn, it halves the effect, to the next 1-5 wounds.
system.hpNote: It cannot be harmed in any way and has no hit points (FF p.51).

system.specialDefenses: Can only be hit by silver and magical weapons
system.description: The huecuva is an undead spirit that looks like a robed skeleton. It is treated as a wight on the cleric/undead matrix, resists all mind-affecting spells, and can polymorph self three times a day. Its touch does 1-6 hit points of damage, and unless the victim saves against poison he catches an acute cardiovascular-renal disease (see disease in the DMG).

The ice lizard looks like a small (3’ long) winged lizard. It lives in cold regions underground and is dull silver.

  • Shape: twice a day it can polymorph self into a white dragon (see the MM, Dragon, White) for two hours at a time. It is manoeuvrability class C in its own form and class E in white dragon form.
  • Spells: sleep and fear, twice a day each.
  • Breath: up to three times a day, a cold breath (like a white dragon’s) for 2-16 hit points.
  • Melee: two claws (1-3 hit points each) and a bite (1-6).
  • Magic: it resists most magic strongly, but is somewhat vulnerable to charm and hold (−2 on saves against each).

In its natural form the imorph is a lumpy grey-green cylinder about 4’ high and 2’ thick on average, the colour of bilious human flesh. A short single leg trails behind with a snail-like suction cup, and more suction cups under the body let it move in jerks. Two 5’ tentacles grow from the top; it has no visible eyes, ears, or other features, and its whole body is a constantly changing mass of rubbery, dough-like material. It does not normally attack unless threatened; when it does, it strikes with its tentacles for 1-4 hit points each.

Imitation: in melee it shows a startling power of imitation.

  • At the start of each melee round except the first, it moves its hit dice and armour class 1 point each toward its opponent’s, gradually changing its shape to match.
  • Its hit points stay the same as its hit dice change, but its chance to hit follows its new hit dice.
  • It copies only appearance. It grows limbs that look like its opponent’s arms and weapons, but still strikes with the equivalent of two tentacles each round for 1-4 hit points each (one may look like an arm wielding a sword and the other an arm holding a shield, for example).
  • When its shape, hit dice, and armour class all match its opponent’s, it immediately adopts the opponent’s attack and movement and switches to the matching attack matrix (the fighter table if it is fighting a human fighting man, for example). It stays on that table until it starts changing back.
  • When the fight ends, or when it is down to 8 hit points or fewer, it changes back by the reverse process, 1 point of armour class and hit dice per melee round.
  • Facing several attackers, it picks one at random to attack and copy. If that “model” dies or retreats, it immediately starts changing to copy another opponent.

Why it is hunted: inside its body is a small organ, like a human liver, made of a rubbery green substance and holding a green liquid. Mixed with an equal amount of water, the liquid works as a potion of polymorph self; one imorph yields enough for 1-3 draughts, which is why adventurers attack them.
system.hpNote: Its hit points stay the same when its hit dice change during combat (FF p.52).

system.description:
The iron cobra is a segmented, snake-shaped automaton of an unknown metal, invented by some great magic-user or minor deity. Only a dozen or so are thought to exist, and they are quite valuable (high-level magic-users rate one at 2,000 gold pieces if deactivated and its control words are known).

  • Control: its creator sets the words that activate and deactivate it; when active it can follow simple spoken commands. Still, it is perfectly silent; moving, it usually makes a soft rustle like a real snake.
  • Tasks: it can guard a treasure, act as a bodyguard, or track down and destroy anyone whose name is known, provided that person is within one mile. It tracks by homing in on the quarry’s psychic vibrations, which a victim aware of the pursuit can block with mind blank or a similar spell.
  • Stealth: it hides in shadows like an 8th-level thief (and infravision cannot spot it, since it gives off no body heat), and can strike with surprise from behind, moving in utter silence for short periods as needed.
  • Bite: 1-3 hit points plus a deadly poison (save at −2). Its fangs hold only enough for three poisonous bites; after that they just do 1-3 hit points. (Its controller, if at hand, can refill the fangs when there is a chance.) Some iron cobras are said to carry a paralysing or sleep-inducing drug instead, against which a normal save applies.
  • Defences: having no mind, it is unaffected by mind-affecting spells (such as sleep or charm), and webs do not affect it. Non-magical weapons do half damage. Against other spells it saves as a 12th-level magic-user.

Jaculi (the word is singular and plural) are agile serpents with chameleon-like camouflage. They live mostly in trees, in woods and forests, eating tree mosses and insects, though some swarms have taken to pillared halls and the like. They are not naturally vicious, but swarms are very territorial and excitable, resenting any more than a passing intrusion into what they see as their territory.

  • Camouflage: there is only 1 chance in 4 of spotting one even in plain view, so they are unlikely to be seen before they attack.
  • Attack: a jaculi has a long, muscular body and a broad, flat head with a ridge of razor-edged bone sticking out on each side. It launches itself from any high point with the force and accuracy of a javelin, surprising its victim unless already spotted. Its “flying speed” is high (51” rate), but after attacking this way it cannot attack from the ground, and must crawl up another tree or pillar before attacking again.

system.treasure: Per 10 individuals O, Q; in lair C, Q (x5), S, T
system.xp: Normal I/7 + 1 per hit point; Elder II/32 + 1 per hit point
system.description:
Jermlaine, also called jinxkins or bane-midges, live in elaborate tunnel and den warrens underground, often very deep. These evil runts are cowardly, attacking only when they can probably overwhelm victims without serious resistance.

Rats: they mix freely with rats of all kinds, even giant ones, and co-operate with them in every way, including defence. 75% of the time rats are with them (01-75 on percentile dice: rats 25%, giant rats 50%), and a lair is 50% likely to have connecting rat tunnels and burrows.

Lairs: they are 60% likely to be within 60’ of their lair when met. The access tunnels are twisting mazes that nothing larger than a gnome can pass, and even a gnome must creep and crawl, exposing itself to attack.

Stealth and senses:

  • They are very fast, with a scuttling gait, very quiet, and masters of staying unseen. Their grey-brown warty hide blends with earth and stone, and they dress in scraps and rags of the same colour. They surprise on 1-5 (d6) and are 75% undetectable when looked or listened for, unless the search is sudden enough to catch them off guard. If a party suddenly goes still and listens carefully, their movement or twittering, squeaking speech can sometimes be heard.
  • Their eyes are weak and their infravision reaches only 30’, but their hearing and smell are keen, so they are 50% likely to detect even invisible creatures in normal dungeon conditions.

Weapons: needle-sharp darts thrown up to 12’ for 1-2 hit points, and a pike-like weapon, a 1½’ wand of supple wood with a sharp metal tip, used as a spear or pike for 1-4 hit points. But they prefer to ambush with pits or nets and take victims alive.

Tactics:

  • They waylay weakened and wounded parties, or careless, sleeping, or lone individuals. Strong groups and alert adventurers are not attacked physically, but jermlaine bands will still try to harm them out of pure malice, which brings the jermlaine gain and may eventually deliver new victims.
  • Traps: in little-used passages they laboriously dig pits under camouflaged trapdoors, or hang nets woven with giant spider silk overhead, and lie in wait. In busier passages they stretch thin but strong cords (often of woven human hair) to trip the unwary.
  • Clubbing: victims not stunned by a trap are beaten senseless with leather clubs full of sand or lead shot while others tie them up. Each blow has a cumulative 2% chance of knocking the victim unconscious, but those in splint, banded, or plate mail are not attacked this way. Well-armoured victims who cannot be tied up are attacked to kill, perhaps with flaming oil or acid.
  • Fate of victims: some are eaten by the jermlaine (or their rat friends), but most humans are stripped naked, shaved, and left tied up and helpless in the passage, while the jermlaine watch from a safe hiding place, waiting for the “fun” of seeing some passing monster eat them.
  • Sabotage: if alert creatures stop near a hidden group, the spiteful things creep out and cut belts, straps, packs, and seams, usually one act each, done quickly so they can escape unseen. The damage is usually noticed only 1-12 turns later, when a weakened strap breaks or a seam opens. Worse, if packs and goods are left where they can reach them, these monstrous little beings foul the water, sour the wine into vinegar, spoil food, desecrate holy water, steal small items (gems, coins, garlic buds, herbs, etc.), wedge daggers or swords so they are hard to draw quickly, cut bowstrings, blunt arrows, puncture oil flasks, and so on.

The old one: if more than 35 are met, one is very old and exceptionally evil, with a very wicked power: he can drain all magic from any magic item (except an artifact or relic) he can handle for 1-4 rounds.

Magic: they count as 4 hit dice creatures for magical attacks and saving throws. Being small and quick, a jermlaine that saves against an attack that would normally do half damage escapes unhurt.

Languages: their own tongue and their alignment language, and they can talk with rats of all kinds. 1 in 10 speaks common, with the same chance for each of dwarvish, gnomish, goblin, and orcish.

Description: they look like tiny humans in baggy clothes and ill-fitting leather helmets. A closer look shows the baggy “clothes” are their lumpy, many-folded skin, and the “helmets” their pointed, evil-looking heads, all leathery and smooth. Their limbs are knotty and bowed, with nimble hands and feet tipped with thick, always filthy nails.
system.hpNote: Treated as 4 hit dice creatures for the effects of magical attacks and saving throws (FF p.54).

system.description:
The much-feared kamadan looks like a large leopard with 4-7 snakes growing from its shoulders. It is clearly a relative of the displacer beast (see the MM, Displacer Beast), though how it became such a strange cross-mutation is anyone’s guess.

  • Melee: two claws (1-3 hit points each) and a bite (1-6). Each snake also bites for 1-4, though the snakes are not poisonous.
  • Breath: a cone of sleep 30’ long and 10’ across at the base. Creatures of 4 dice or less fall asleep with no saving throw; creatures with more hit dice save as against dragon breath.

Kelpies are intelligent water plants that in their own shape look like a heap of wet seaweed. They can reshape their bodies into any form, and often take the shape of a beautiful woman to lure men into deep water; they have also been known to look like a horse. But whatever the shape, the substance is still green seaweed, and the effect is rather grotesque.

Charm: to make up for this, a kelpie can cast one powerful charm per day. A victim who fails to save against spells (at −2) sees the kelpie as the most wonderful, perfect, desirable woman (or steed) and willingly leaps into the water to join her (or reach it).

  • The kelpie wraps itself around the charmed man, who tries to breathe water and sinks with it in an ecstasy of drowning. Left alone, he drowns happily and is dragged off to the kelpie’s lair to be eaten.
  • Even if the kelpie cannot reach him, he still tries to swim down and breathe water. A charmed victim trying to drown takes 2-20 hit points per melee round until he comes up for air or dies.
  • Killing the kelpie breaks the charm at once.
  • Females are immune. Legend says the sea-god made kelpies to punish men rash enough to sail the oceans without paying him proper respect; women had no part in those offences and so did not earn his anger. Others say Olhydra, the Elemental Princess of Evil Water Creatures, made the kelpies and spared females out of regard for her own sex.
  • Habitat: oceans and seas, dismal swamps, and stagnant underground grottos; sometimes almost any deep body of water, even man-made. They can leave the water to walk on land for short periods (1-3 hours at most).
  • Fire: being slimy and wet, they take only half damage from fire (none on a successful save).
  • They are very cunning and try to pick off stragglers, lone watchmen, or the last members of groups whenever they can.

system.xp: 2HD: II/28 + 2 per hit point; 3HD: III/120 + 3 per hit point; 4HD: IV/240 + 4 per hit point; 5HD: V/420 + 5 per hit point
system.description:
Kenku are winged, two-legged bird-people with clawed hands and feet and a hawk’s head with a sharp beak. They are mischievous, habitually using their limited magic to annoy and inconvenience humans, though they do not usually mean to kill. They are manoeuvrability class D in aerial combat.

  • Fighting: every kenku has the thieving abilities of a 4th-level thief, and they are expert fighters, usually with a quarterstaff or a samurai sword. Unarmed, they use two claws (1-4 hit points each) and a vicious bite (1-6).
  • Disguise: they disguise themselves well and pass for human with only a 50% chance of detection (though the length of the nose usually gives them away).
  • Speech: they do not speak, and seem to communicate with each other telepathically.

Groups: a small group has two of 2HD and two of 3HD, or three and two respectively. A group of 6 or 7 has a leader of 4HD, two of 3HD, and three or four of 2HD. A group of 8 has a supreme leader of 5HD.

Magic by hit dice (the innate abilities come with age and suitable training):

  • 3HD: one 1st-level magic-user spell (often magic missile), and innate shape change once every 30 days; after 7 days in the new shape they must resume their own. Particularly bold kenku have used it to take the form of a god and accept offerings from gullible worshippers, one example of the bizarre uses kenku, especially the young, find for it.
  • 4HD: as 3HD, plus another 1st-level magic-user spell (usually shocking grasp) and innate invisibility with no limit on how often or how long. These too are sometimes put to odd uses, but 4HD kenku tend to be older and less reckless.
  • 5HD: as 4HD, plus a 2nd-level magic-user spell (usually mirror image or web), and they may call lightning, an innate ability with the same effects as the 3rd-level druid spell.
  • Kenku of more than 5HD, with even greater magic, are rumoured to exist.

Dealings with humans: kenku favour kidnapping as a source of money. They give treasure freely, but it is rarely real and crumbles to worthless dust within a day. They appear helpful and offer non-verbal advice, usually carefully designed to mislead and tempt the party into danger or trouble. As a rough guide, the chance of a kenku actually helping humans is about 5%, varying with circumstances.

Lairs: those found so far are small underground caverns, but larger caverns deeper underground are thought to hold larger numbers in a formal social structure.

Khargra come from the Elemental Plane of Earth and sometimes enter the Prime Material Plane looking for high-grade ores to eat. They “swim” through layers of rock in small schools, riding earth movements and the shifting of rock strata as if swimming, or surfing, in the sea. Fortunately they are very rarely seen on the Prime Material Plane, and can usually be appeased by immediately handing over all metal items.

Feeding: finding a suitable vein, they settle down to eat, grinding up the ore and, through their strange digestion, separating and refining the metal. The slag is excreted, and the metal stored in internal reservoirs to be absorbed slowly. Naturally they prefer refined metal to ore, and if they sense some reasonably close by they abandon their normal diet for it. Armour and weapons are a tasty meal, and they especially love “eating” metal treasure.

  • Ambush: they leap from the wall or floor of a cavern or passage like fish leaping from water, flying up to 10’, and try to clamp onto large metal objects with their clawed arms to devour them. These attacks surprise nearby adventurers on 1-7 (d8), or 1-5 (d6) if dwarves or gnomes are present.
  • Eating: one khargra can swallow up to 5 pounds (50 gold pieces weight) of metal per melee round and holds 100 pounds or sometimes more.
  • Out of rock: once in the open air they must crawl, pulling themselves along with their arms.
  • Fighting: if attacked, a khargra fights back, annoyed at being disturbed while eating. On any roll of 16 or better it bites the end off a metal weapon used against it and swallows it. Against non-metal opponents it bites powerfully for 3-18 hit points, though its attacks are only incidental to its main aim of eating metal. At least one of its three strong clawed arms must “hit” a victim (each hits as a 12HD creature) before it can bite him; the arms do no damage, but once one grips, it does not let go until the way to the metal it wants is clear or the victim is dead. Khargra have been known to bite right through large fleshy creatures to reach metal beyond.
  • Treasure: cutting a dead khargra open (far from easy) reveals up to 500 gold pieces weight of unabsorbed metal pebbles in its unique digestive system, reflecting its recent diet; they may be any metal, including precious ones.

Weaknesses and immunities:

  • It leaves rock instantly, but takes a full melee round to merge back into it. Phase door cast on it during that round kills it instantly, and the body stays out of phase until the magic is dispelled.
  • Transmute metal to wood also kills a khargra.
  • It is immune to fire and cold spells except heat metal, which always does maximum damage. Lightning does full damage.
  • Move earth stops it in its tracks, stunning and confusing it for 1-3 melee rounds.

Description: khargra are about 3½’ long, cylindrical, tapering toward the rear, and weigh about 300 pounds. Three large, flexible metal fins are spaced evenly around the body, running lengthwise. Between the fins are three conical sheaths from which extending clawed arms reach up to 3’ from the body. Small eye-bulges stick out on each side of the top fin. The mouth, a full foot across, is lined with curved, razor-sharp metal teeth that open and close it like an iris. The body is covered in large metal scales.

Killmoulis always live where some industry goes on, preferably one involving grain or other food. They live under floors, in cracks in walls, or among dark rafters, coming out only when the human workers leave. Then, like brownies, they work and make themselves useful, while eating huge amounts of meal, flour, grain, or whatever food is there.

  • Tricks: playing tricks and practical jokes is part of their nature. If the inhabitants molest any killmoulis, the tricks will certainly be destructive or harmful; otherwise they are merely bothersome and irritating, without undue destruction.
  • Stealth: they are very fast and can blend into their surroundings and hide in shadows so well they are nearly undetectable (only 10% chance).
  • Enemies: they hate dogs and cats almost as much as rats, since all of these attack them. They snare or kill rats with long pins, and usually poison threatening dogs and cats with whatever poison is at hand. If they cannot kill the cats, dogs, and rats that threaten them, they move elsewhere.

A killmoulis is small, usually under a foot tall, with a thin body and limbs but a large head with matching ears. It has no mouth; it draws food in through its huge nose. They seem to communicate with each other telepathically.

system.treasure: Individuals L, M, N; in lair, Z
system.description:
History: the ancient kuo-toa people once lived on the shores and islands of the upper world, but as mankind and its allied races grew more numerous and powerful, these “mer-fish” were slowly pushed into remote regions. Constant war on these evil, human-sacrificing creatures threatened to wipe them out, since several powerful beings were helping their sworn enemy, mankind. Some kuo-toans fled to sea caverns and secret underground waters, and while their kin above were slaughtered, these few prospered and adapted to their lightless homes. The deep-sea kuo-toans were in turn wiped out by other fierce, evil sea creatures, leaving only those in the underworld to carry on the race. Men came to forget them entirely; even “goggler”, a mocking name for these fish-like foes, lost its meaning. But the underworld kuo-toans never forgot, and woe to the human who falls into their slimy clutches.

Today they hate sunlight and are almost never met on the surface. That, and their inborn dislike of discipline, keeps them from rising again, though they have become numerous once more and gained new powers. They have also become somewhat unstable, and insanity is not uncommon among them. Small groups sometimes travel to the upper world to kidnap humans as slaves and sacrifices, and such parties are occasionally met in dungeons connected to the vast system of underworld passages and caverns that honeycombs the earth’s crust. Only far below the surface, in natural caverns and spaces carved from the rock over the ages, do they build their communities.

Bands: they usually travel in well-armed bands. If more than 20 are met, they are 50% likely to be within 1-6 miles of their lair.

  • Per 4 normal warriors: an extra fighter of 3rd or 4th level.
  • Per 8 normal fighters: an extra fighter of 5th or 6th level.
  • Per 12 in the group: a cleric/assassin of equal levels, 4th/4th, 5th/5th, 6th/6th, or 7th/7th (d4 + 3 decides the level).

War parties: a group with more than 20 normal (2nd level) fighters is a war party, a full-scale raiding force, and also includes:

  • 1 10th level fighter as “captain”
  • 2 8th level fighters as “lieutenants”
  • 4 3rd/3rd level fighter/assassin “whips”
  • 1 “monitor” (see below)
  • 1 slave per 4 kuo-toans

The whips are fanatical devotees of Sea Mother, the kuo-toan goddess, who inspire the troops to stand firm and fight without quarter for the glory of their ruler and their deity.

Lairs: a lair has 40-400 2nd level males, higher-level fighters in the same ratios as outside groups, war parties, and:

  • a priest-king (12th/12th level cleric/assassin) if there are 350 or more normal kuo-toans; or a priest-duke of 11th/11th level if there are 275-349; or a priest-prince of 10th/10th level if fewer than 275;
  • 8 “eyes” of the priest-king, -duke, or -prince: 8th/8th (or 7th/7th or 6th/6th) level cleric/assassins;
  • 1 “chief whip”: 6th/6th level fighter/assassin;
  • 2 “whips” of 4th/4th or 5th/5th level;
  • 1 “monitor” per 20 2nd level males;
  • females equal to 20% of the males;
  • young (non-combatant) equal to 20% of all kuo-toans;
  • slaves equal to 50% of the males.

Religious communities: special religious places also have kuo-toan clerics, in addition to everyone else: a 3rd level cleric per 20 individuals, a 4th level cleric per 40, and a 5th level cleric per 80. They are headed by:

  • 1 6th level cleric if the group is 160 or fewer;
  • 1 7th level and 1 6th level cleric if it is 161-240;
  • 1 8th level, 1 7th level, and 1 6th level if it is 241-320;
  • 1 9th level, 2 7th level, and 3 6th level if it is 321-400;
  • 1 10th level, 2 8th level, and 4 6th level if it is over 400.

Pincer staff: any kuo-toan cleric above 6th level is 50% likely to carry one: a 5’ pole topped by a 3’ “claw”, like a medieval man-catcher. A hit means the claw has closed on the opponent, who cannot get free. (It works only on creatures about the girth of a small to large human, from elf to gnoll size.) It is 10% likely to pin both arms and 40% likely to pin only one (for a right-handed victim, the left 75% of the time, the right 25%). A trapped opponent loses all shield and dexterity protection (or, if his weapon arm is trapped, his weapon attacks; he still loses dexterity protection but keeps his shield), and nearby kuo-toans always strike at trapped individuals.

Growth and hit points: kuo-toans spawn like fish. The hatchlings, called “fingerlings”, are raised in pools until they become amphibious about a year after hatching. The young, now about 1’ tall, can then breathe air and are raised in groups by sex and fitness. Their breeding gives every kuo-toan exactly the same hit points per die, by level:

Weapons: typical arms of kuo-toan fighters:

  • dagger, spear, and shield: 40%
  • dagger, spear, and weighted throwing net: 30%
  • dagger and harpoon*: 10%
  • dagger and short bow (half the female population): 20%

* Usually only higher-level fighters use the harpoon, a wickedly barbed throwing weapon with a range of 30’, doing 2-12 hit points (before bonuses). A creature struck must roll 13 or better on d20 to avoid being snagged. Snagged creatures of man-size or less are jerked off their feet and stunned for 1-4 rounds, while the kuo-toan, whose harpoon is tied to him by a stout cord, hauls the victim in and tries to kill him with a dagger thrust.

Shields: made of special boiled leather and coated just before battle with a particularly sticky glue. Any frontal attack on a shield-bearer has a 25% chance of hitting the glue and sticking fast until the wielder pulls it free (the same chance he has of opening a dungeon door). Shields do not add to a kuo-toan’s armour class; they are used as weapons.

Combat:

  • They wear no clothes, only leather harnesses for weapons and a little personal gear, since anything else would hinder swimming. Their tough, scaly, very slimy skin, with their dexterity, gives them a good natural armour class.
  • They hit as humans of the same level, but males get +1 to hit and damage with weapons because of their strength (not with their bite, which does 2-5 hit points). When fighting with only a dagger, they can also bite.
  • Lightning: two or more kuo-toan clerics or cleric/assassins joining hands can produce a stroke of lightning. The bolt is very narrow, hitting only the chosen target unless another creature happens to get into its 2’ wide path. It does 6 hit points per cleric or cleric/assassin taking part (half on a save). The chance of producing it is 10% per round per kuo-toan involved, cumulative (check each round they act together).

Defences:

  • Their slimy skin makes attempts to grapple, grasp, tie, or web them only 25% likely to succeed.
  • Their eyes, on the sides of the head, see independently with a very wide field (180°), and detect movement even of creatures that are magically invisible, astrally projected, or ethereal; only complete stillness escapes their notice. They see into the infrared and ultraviolet and can feel vibrations within 10”, so they are surprised only on 1 (in 6).
  • They are completely immune to poison and paralysis. Spells that affect only humanoid-type creatures (charm person, hold person, sleep, and so on) do not affect them. Electricity does half damage (none on a save). A magic missile does only 1 hit point, and all illusions are useless against them.
  • But they hate bright light, such as from a light spell, and fight at −1 to hit in it. They take full damage from fire and save against it at −2.

Priests and monitors: especially fit fingerlings, usually of noble spawning, are trained for the priesthood as clerics, cleric/assassins, or special celibate monks. These monks are “monitors”, who control community members who turn violent or go insane. A monitor can attack to subdue or to kill. It has 56 hit points, attacks at 7th level, and has:

  • twice normal movement rate;
  • surprised only on 1 in 10;
  • armour class 1;
  • 4 attacks per round: 2 bare-handed for 2-8 hit points (double if subduing) and 2 bites for 2-5, one set of hands and bite early in the round and the second late in it.
  • It can subdue creatures no larger than man-sized or slightly larger (up to 8’ tall/500 pounds). Subduing attacks do only half actual damage, but when the hit points scored equal the creature’s total, it is knocked unconscious for 3-12 rounds.

Relations: separate communities do not usually co-operate, though they share special religious places for trade between groups, councils, and the worship of Sea Mother, open to all kuo-toans. These places, and other settlements, are open to the drow and their servants, who provide useful goods and services as slave traders and merchants; but the kuo-toans both fear and hate the drow, so kidnappings and minor skirmishes are frequent. They greatly hate illithids (mind flayers; see the MM, Mind Flayer) and attack them and their allies on sight. Despite this shared hatred, they are not on good terms with the githyanki, whom they deeply distrust and avoid as best they can. They always attack githzerai.

Slaves are used for labour, food, and sacrifice. Roll for each slave’s race:

Languages: the underground trade language common to most intelligent underworld dwellers, plus their own arcane tongue; they can also communicate with most fish by empathy. Their religious speech is a corrupted form of the language of the Elemental Plane of Water. If a cleric is nearby, any creature from that plane is 75% unlikely to attack kuo-toans, because the cleric will speak to it and ask that they be spared in the name of Sea Mother (Blibdoolpoolp).

Description: a kuo-toan looks cold and horrible, much like a paunchy human body covered in scales, with a fish’s head set squarely on its shoulders. Its huge fish eyes tend to swivel in different directions as it looks around. The hands and feet are very long, with three fingers and an opposable digit, partly webbed; the arms and legs are short for the body. They are pale grey, with undertones of tan or yellow in males only, and the whole skin has a sheen from its slime. The colour darkens when the creature is angry and pales when it is badly frightened.
system.hpNote: Kuo-toans have fixed hit points for their hit dice (FF p.58). A monitor has 56 hit points and attacks at 7th level.

system.description:
Lamia nobles rule other lamias and the wild, lonely areas they live in. Unlike the normal lamia (see the MM, Lamia), a lamia noble has the lower body of a giant serpent and an upper body that may be male or female. They are given to outbursts of senseless violence.

  • Males wield short swords and have magical ability at experience level 1-6, plus the spells charm person, mirror image, suggestion, and illusion.
  • Females carry no weapons and attack only with spells, but are more experienced magically, with abilities at experience level 2-8 plus the same spells.
  • Touch: it permanently drains 1 point of wisdom. When a victim’s wisdom falls below 3, he willingly does whatever the lamia noble tells him.
  • Human form: all can take human form (though intelligent humanoids always see through the disguise) and so try to slip into human society to do evil. In human form, they are recognised as lamias only by humans and demi-humans of 7th level or above (10% chance per level above 6th, cumulative, with clerics getting a flat 15% extra).
  • They speak all the languages of the man-like races.

system.xp: 4HD: III/150 + 4 per hit point; 5HD: IV/205 + 5 per hit point; Spell-casters: V/280 + 5 per hit point; Double-classed: V/475 + 6 per hit point; Triple-classed: VI/700 + 7 per hit point
system.description:
Lava children are humanoids about the size of a broadly built man, but strangely childlike in look, with pinkish-white skin and a permanent smile. They are the unnatural offspring of a union between spirits of earth and fire. They live underground or in volcanic regions, and speak their own hissing tongue and common.

  • Attacks: two clawed hands (1-6 hit points each) and a surprisingly powerful bite (2-12).
  • Metal: they are strangely “immune” to metal; for them, metal simply does not exist. Metal objects pass through them harmlessly, and they move through metal unhindered. Metal worn by their victims is ignored when working out armour class.
  • Magic: completely immune to fire and earth magic, but vulnerable to air and water magic, taking one extra hit point per caster level from the latter.

Groups: most have 4 hit dice and are fighters, but some are exceptional:

  • 3-7: one “warrior”, a higher-level fighter of 5 hit dice who hits at +1.
  • 8-10: one warrior and one magic-user, also of 5 hit dice.
  • 11-14: one warrior, one magic-user, and one cleric, each of 5 hit dice.
  • 15-18: all the above plus one double-classed warrior/magic-user of 6 hit dice.
  • Their highest leaders are said to be triple-classed warrior/magic-user/clerics of 7 hit dice.

Spells: magic-users can use each of these once per day, at 6th level of magic use: affect normal fires, burning hands, feather fall, light, fools gold, pyrotechnics, fireball, and slow. Clerics can use cure light wounds, light, remove fear, find traps (×2), slow poison, continual light, and dispel magic.
system.hpNote: The hit dice of triple-classed leaders are not given (FF p.61).

system.description:
The lizard king is a kind of lizard man (see the MM), taller, more intelligent, and more human-like than a normal one. Apart from the exceptions noted here, it has all the traits of a normal lizard man. It lives in damp places, usually near an underground river or lake.

  • Followers: it has 10-100 lizard men followers and guards, from whom it demands two human sacrifices each week. They always make every effort to meet this demand, since a king without human sacrifices to eat substitutes two of its followers for each missing human.
  • Trident: its fearsome trident does 5-20 hit points. If the to-hit roll beats the score needed by 5 or more, it skewers the victim, doing double normal damage, at least 15 hit points. These special properties work only for lizard kings; sages have puzzled over this for years without reaching any conclusion, but in human hands it is just a normal trident.

system.specialAttacks: Energy and strength drain - see below
system.specialDefenses: Can only be hit by silver and magical weapons; and see below
system.description:
Only three or four of these creatures are believed to exist. They were summoned to the Prime Material Plane and stranded there by an evil, high-level magic-user who died from the strain of the summoning; their home plane is unknown. Everything they do is driven by the need to occupy the body of a character of 5th or higher level to perform the complex ritual that will return them home. Only a human body gives them the psychic frame of reference they need, so they attack only humans.

Appearance: a cylinder of white flame 5’ tall and 3’ across, with a wispy tail 5’ long, though it gives off no noticeable heat.

The attack:

  1. Flash: moving at extraordinary speed, it approaches a party with humans in it and gets within 10’ of its chosen victim (picked at random among the humans). There it pauses and flares in a split-second, blinding flash of white light. Everyone within 20’ who is looking at it (non-humans included) must save versus petrification or be blinded for 12 turns (two full hours); treat as the illusionist spell blindness.
  2. First hit: it then attacks, automatically winning initiative every round, even against hasted opponents. A hit drains one energy level and two points of strength (the strength comes back at 1 point per hour; the level drain is permanent) and does 3-12 hit points.
  3. Merging: once it hits, it is locked onto the victim and gradually merges into his body, draining energy and strength and doing 3-12 hit points each round, automatically with no to-hit roll. After two rounds of merging, the only way to hit the spirit without harming the victim is holy water, doing 2-7 hit points per vial and forcing it to stop merging (though it may attack the same or another human the next round).
  4. Takeover: after three rounds of merging without being forced off (two rounds vulnerable to normal attack, then one vulnerable only to holy water), it has taken over the victim and the human mind is gone.
    • If the victim still has five or more energy levels (hit dice) by then (he will have lost four, one from the first hit and three from merging, so he must have been at least 9th level), the spirit uses the body to shriek out its spell, taking 5 segments, and body and spirit vanish in a flash of light. The spirit has gone home, never to return.
    • If he has fewer than five left (so was 8th level or lower), the spirit abandons the body and turns on another nearby human, if there is one, starting all over again.

The first victim’s body, now a mindless husk, collapses and resists all attempts at resurrection (though a powerful spell such as wish, properly used, will bring him back).

Defences: only silver or magical weapons harm it. It has 50% magic resistance and is immune to sleep, charm, hold, paralysation, and fear spells. Holy water harms it at any time, merging or not, doing 2-7 hit points per vial thrown on it.

This flying creature looks much like a sea ray, with a flat body about 3’ long (and nearly as wide) and a thin, whip-like tail 4’ long. The mantari (singular and plural) is found in most kinds of places, though it prefers dirty dungeon chambers full of its prey. It usually feeds on giant rats and the like, but is normally (85%) aggressive toward other creatures and humans. It is manoeuvrability class C in aerial combat.

  • Attack: it flies with its tail hanging straight down, but when it attacks, diving on its victim from 10’-12’ above the ground, it holds the tail forward at an acute angle to its body. It strikes only by whipping the victim with its tail.
  • Sting: the sting at the tip is not poisonous but attacks the nervous system. A hit does damage equal to 19 minus the victim’s constitution (a victim with constitution 12 takes 7 hit points). There is no saving throw.
  • Repeated hits: if it hits the same victim in two melee rounds in a row, the second hit does four times normal damage. Third and later successive hits on the same victim also do four times normal, with no further increase.

Meazels are solitary bipeds a little under man-size, rarely met outside their lairs in marshes or small, dank underground caves, and rarely straying far from them. They are traditional enemies of orcs and kobolds, and most underworld creatures attack them, since they have a nasty reputation even among dungeon dwellers.

  • Thieving: they have natural thieving abilities at 4th level. They rarely attack openly, preferring to hide and, moving quietly and swiftly, strangle stragglers from behind or pick pockets for the gold they love.
  • Claws: two, for 1-4 hit points each.
  • Strangling cord: alternatively, a tough, thin cord. A “hit” means it is round the victim’s neck, and he dies of strangulation within two melee rounds unless he breaks free, or the meazel dies or has to let go (to defend itself from another attacker, for example). It can do this only to a victim of man-size or smaller, and only by approaching from behind undetected and gaining surprise.
  • Lair: it takes all corpses there to eat in safety. Piles of sacks full of bones are often found near a lair. Any gems the meazel has found are in these sacks, since it does not recognise the value of precious and semi-precious stones; for the same reason there are no gems in the lair itself.

Description: skin from light grey to dark green. Most (85%) have irregular patches of angry red from a skin disease common in the species (harmless beyond the disfigurement, and not contagious) that makes them look almost leprous. The eyes are jet black and the feet partly webbed.

Meenlocks are small bipeds about 2’ tall, covered in shaggy black fur, with white heads cut by dark ridges. They look so horrible that anyone of four or fewer hit dice who sees them is struck with fear and falls inert to the ground for 5-8 melee rounds (half that on a successful save). They are highly evil and hungry for vengeance on humankind.

The shaft: they live in dark, sealed, vertical shafts underground. If the seal is removed, the bottom cannot be seen, and anything dropped lands silently on a thick carpet of moss lining the walls and floor. The shaft is dark, a smell of rotting corpses drifts up, and anyone but the most insensitive feels a strong emanation of evil even without detect evil. After about 20’ straight down, the shaft twists and curves, so even a light spell reveals only the upper part.

In the lair: adventurers who brave the shaft eventually find the lair, a space like a small cave at the very bottom.

  • Meenlocks always attack there (except that bright light makes them flee if they can), using two claws for 1-4 hit points each. Their touch paralyses (saving throw applies).
  • At close quarters, as in the lair, their telepathy is nearly useless; that is why they deliberately create the smell of rotting corpses, to keep intruders out.
  • They are very clever at putting out torches, lanterns, and other lights.
  • Every other melee round they can dimension door up to 6’, and while doing so attacks on them are at −4 to hit. They cannot do this while carrying a victim; it takes three meenlocks to carry one.

Marking a victim: they do best when adventurers unseal the shaft but then fail to get into the lair. When the party leaves, meenlocks follow at a safe distance, climbing the shaft quickly and silently thanks to the deadening moss. They “mark” one adventurer, chosen at random (a paladin first, if one is present; always a human if there is one, otherwise an elf, dwarf, or other near-human), and direct all their later attacks at him alone.

  • From then on the victim gets disturbing telepathic messages (they can communicate telepathically up to 300’). The wording varies but the threat is always the same: the meenlocks are hunting him relentlessly and mean to make him one of them. He is also aware of stealthy movement in the shadows and rustling, scratching noises, all illusory and telepathically induced. His companions hear and notice nothing, and may decide he is mentally unbalanced.
  • Until the party beds down, he grows more and more preoccupied and less able to concentrate on the adventure. The referee decides the exact effects, but as a guide, for each hour of harassment his strength, dexterity, intelligence, and wisdom each drop by 1 point temporarily, he attacks at −1 to hit in melee, and victims of his spells (if he is a spell-caster) get +2 on their saves. All these effects are cumulative, but vanish as soon as the meenlock threat is somehow removed (for example, if the party moves into a brightly lit area the meenlocks cannot enter).

The final attack: once the party beds down to rest, the meenlocks attack, moving very silently (80% chance of surprise even against a watchful guard, 100% against a sleeper). They try to silence any guards and drag their victim away; they will not claw the victim unless they must, but show no such mercy to anyone else. If they succeed, they take him to their shaft and seal it behind them. After a short but gruesome treatment, the victim himself becomes a meenlock.

Mephits are the evil messengers and errand-runners of the powerful beings of the Lower Planes, and are common in all of them, from the Nine Hells to the Abyss. Their alignment depends on their plane of origin, but is always evil. No type is known to be more or less common on any particular Lower Plane; they seem to be spread at random. Other kinds are thought to exist, but none has yet been positively identified.

  • Missions: on the Prime Material Plane they always have some demonic or diabolic mission (or one from a similar evil power). This may be demanding, such as finding a particular victim and capturing him to be taken to Hades, or general, such as indiscriminate looting and killing.
  • Character: mephits are connoisseurs of the vulgar and tasteless, with a deeply twisted sense of humour (to a mephit, a creature writhing in agony is excruciatingly funny). They especially enjoy tormenting the helpless. When they can get them (as they usually do), they wear clothes of the gaudiest possible design and colour, and are often seen puffing on smoking rolls of very foul-smelling dried plants. They strut, and have shrill voices.
  • All mephits are about 5’ tall, with working wings and fangs, and are manoeuvrability class B in aerial combat. They all speak a common mephit tongue and their alignment language.

Fire mephit: dull red streaked thinly with black, its body wreathed in wisps of flame; touching it bare-handed does 1 hit point of damage.

  • Claws: two, for 1-3 hit points each plus 1 point of heat (2-4 in total).
  • Breath (three times a day), in either of two forms as it chooses: a jet of flame 15’ long and 1’ across that automatically hits a chosen target in range for 2-9 hit points (half on a save); or a blanket of flame 5’ square directly in front of it, doing 4 hit points to each victim (no save).
  • Spells: heat metal and magic missile (2 missiles), once each per day.
  • Gate: once every hour it may try to gate in another mephit (25% chance), of fire, lava, smoke, or steam type (equally likely).

Lava mephit: dull red, constantly oozing small drops of molten lava like very heavy sweat. Its heat can be felt 30’ away, and touching it with bare flesh does 1-8 hit points.

  • Claws: 1 hit point each plus 1-8 of heat (2-9 in total).
  • Breath: a blob of molten lava that automatically hits any single chosen target within 10’ for 1-6 hit points (no save), usable once every three rounds. Away from molten lava it can spit at most 8 blobs; once that “supply” is used up it cannot breathe again that day unless it recharges by touching molten lava.
  • Regeneration: in volcanic areas with molten lava available, it regenerates 2 hit points per round just by staying in contact with the lava (this stops when it is killed).
  • Dissolving touch: its touch automatically dissolves materials, wood slowly (only one inch thickness per hour) and metals quickly (plate armour in 3 melee rounds).
  • Shape: all lava mephits can change at will into a pool of molten lava (this does not recharge the breath weapon).
  • Gate: once per hour it may try to gate in 1-2 other mephits (each type equally likely; if two come they are the same type), with a 25% chance of success.

Smoke mephit: black, with smoke oozing from its body. On the Prime Material Plane it stays in smoky, dark places and never comes into bright light unless forced to.

  • Claws: two, for 1-2 hit points each.
  • Breath: a sooty ball of smoke that automatically hits any single chosen victim within 20’ for 1-4 hit points (no save) and blinds him for 1-2 melee rounds. It can breathe every other melee round, with no limit on the total.
  • Spells: invisibility and dancing lights, once each per day.
  • Gate: once every hour it may try to gate in 1-2 other mephits (each type equally likely; if two come they are the same type), with a 20% chance of success.
  • Death: when it dies it coughs up flame doing 1 hit point to everyone within 10’ (no save).

Steam mephit: grey, constantly oozing hot water and leaving a trail of water wherever it goes. Touching it with bare flesh does 1 hit point, with a 50% chance of being stunned for one melee round.

  • Claws: two, for 1-4 hit points each.
  • Breath: a jet of scalding water that automatically hits any single chosen victim within 20’ for 1-3 hit points (no save), with a 50% chance of stunning him for one melee round. It can use this without limit, once every two melee rounds.
  • Rainstorm: once a day, a “rainstorm” of boiling water; treat as ice storm doing 2-12 hit points to all victims (no saves).
  • Contaminate water: once per hour (the reverse of purify water).
  • Gate: once per hour it may try to gate in 1-2 other mephits (each type equally likely; if two come they are the same type), with a 30% chance of success.

Fire mephit: dull red streaked thinly with black, its body wreathed in wisps of flame; touching it bare-handed does 1 hit point of damage.

  • Claws: two, for 1-3 hit points each plus 1 point of heat (2-4 in total).
  • Breath (three times a day), in either of two forms as it chooses: a jet of flame 15’ long and 1’ across that automatically hits a chosen target in range for 2-9 hit points (half on a save); or a blanket of flame 5’ square directly in front of it, doing 4 hit points to each victim (no save).
  • Spells: heat metal and magic missile (2 missiles), once each per day.
  • Gate: once every hour it may try to gate in another mephit (25% chance), of fire, lava, smoke, or steam type (equally likely).

Lava mephit: dull red, constantly oozing small drops of molten lava like very heavy sweat. Its heat can be felt 30’ away, and touching it with bare flesh does 1-8 hit points.

  • Claws: 1 hit point each plus 1-8 of heat (2-9 in total).
  • Breath: a blob of molten lava that automatically hits any single chosen target within 10’ for 1-6 hit points (no save), usable once every three rounds. Away from molten lava it can spit at most 8 blobs; once that “supply” is used up it cannot breathe again that day unless it recharges by touching molten lava.
  • Regeneration: in volcanic areas with molten lava available, it regenerates 2 hit points per round just by staying in contact with the lava (this stops when it is killed).
  • Dissolving touch: its touch automatically dissolves materials, wood slowly (only one inch thickness per hour) and metals quickly (plate armour in 3 melee rounds).
  • Shape: all lava mephits can change at will into a pool of molten lava (this does not recharge the breath weapon).
  • Gate: once per hour it may try to gate in 1-2 other mephits (each type equally likely; if two come they are the same type), with a 25% chance of success.

Smoke mephit: black, with smoke oozing from its body. On the Prime Material Plane it stays in smoky, dark places and never comes into bright light unless forced to.

  • Claws: two, for 1-2 hit points each.
  • Breath: a sooty ball of smoke that automatically hits any single chosen victim within 20’ for 1-4 hit points (no save) and blinds him for 1-2 melee rounds. It can breathe every other melee round, with no limit on the total.
  • Spells: invisibility and dancing lights, once each per day.
  • Gate: once every hour it may try to gate in 1-2 other mephits (each type equally likely; if two come they are the same type), with a 20% chance of success.
  • Death: when it dies it coughs up flame doing 1 hit point to everyone within 10’ (no save).

Steam mephit: grey, constantly oozing hot water and leaving a trail of water wherever it goes. Touching it with bare flesh does 1 hit point, with a 50% chance of being stunned for one melee round.

  • Claws: two, for 1-4 hit points each.
  • Breath: a jet of scalding water that automatically hits any single chosen victim within 20’ for 1-3 hit points (no save), with a 50% chance of stunning him for one melee round. It can use this without limit, once every two melee rounds.
  • Rainstorm: once a day, a “rainstorm” of boiling water; treat as ice storm doing 2-12 hit points to all victims (no saves).
  • Contaminate water: once per hour (the reverse of purify water).
  • Gate: once per hour it may try to gate in 1-2 other mephits (each type equally likely; if two come they are the same type), with a 30% chance of success.

Mephits are the evil messengers and errand-runners of the powerful beings of the Lower Planes, and are common in all of them, from the Nine Hells to the Abyss. Their alignment depends on their plane of origin, but is always evil. No type is known to be more or less common on any particular Lower Plane; they seem to be spread at random. Other kinds are thought to exist, but none has yet been positively identified.

  • Missions: on the Prime Material Plane they always have some demonic or diabolic mission (or one from a similar evil power). This may be demanding, such as finding a particular victim and capturing him to be taken to Hades, or general, such as indiscriminate looting and killing.
  • Character: mephits are connoisseurs of the vulgar and tasteless, with a deeply twisted sense of humour (to a mephit, a creature writhing in agony is excruciatingly funny). They especially enjoy tormenting the helpless. When they can get them (as they usually do), they wear clothes of the gaudiest possible design and colour, and are often seen puffing on smoking rolls of very foul-smelling dried plants. They strut, and have shrill voices.
  • All mephits are about 5’ tall, with working wings and fangs, and are manoeuvrability class B in aerial combat. They all speak a common mephit tongue and their alignment language.
