Mezzodaemons live in numbers on the Lower Planes between the Abyss and the Hells: Tarterus, Hades, and Gehenna. They mix freely with night hags and demons (see the MM), and do not mind devils, though they find devils’ strict rules very tiresome. They sometimes roam the Astral and Ethereal Planes, and are not too hard to summon to the Prime Material Plane, since they enjoy wreaking havoc there and will work with evil humans and the like if the price is right and their “superior” standing is acknowledged.

  • Fighting: they use their 18(00) strength to great effect. Their horny hands and talons strike for 7-12 hit points per blow, but a mezzodaemon often uses a magic weapon (battle-axe, flail, or bastard or two-handed sword), usually with a magic shield, and is +3 to hit when so armed.
  • Magic items: they can use almost any magic item not limited by alignment or class (books, librams, tomes, and similar magic affecting the reader are excluded). But their own magic resistance gives such items varying chances of failing, so they tend to avoid all but powerful ones.
  • Powers: dimension door (twice a day), become ethereal (once a day), magic jar (once a day), passwall (four times a day), repulsion (once a day), wind walk (once a day), and word of recall (once a day). At will, one per melee round: comprehend languages, detect invisibility, detect magic, ESP, invisibility, levitate, polymorph self, and read magic.
  • Defences: unaffected by non-magical weapons (including iron and silver), paralysis, and poison of any kind. Acid, cold, and fire do half damage. They can never be charmed, and suggestion never affects them.
  • Magic resistance depends on the spell level: 95% against 1st-level spells, 90% against 2nd, 85% against 3rd, and so on down to 55% against 9th. This assumes an 11th-level caster and goes up or down for casters of lower or higher level.
  • Senses: they see into the infrared and ultraviolet, and a limited telepathy lets them communicate with any creature of low intelligence or better.

Each mezzodaemon has its own name, which it keeps very secret to avoid being commanded by nycadaemons, demon lords, arch-devils, and the like, or trapped by a summoning spell.

Mites are humanoids only 2’ tall, with large heads and evil faces, and skin from light grey to violet. They live in networks of narrow tunnels above and below the main dungeon corridors. Adventurers often hear their scurrying feet and high-pitched twittering, but rarely see them, and they never attack openly. They are related to jermlaine and snyads, and seem to have no real language; their twittering conveys only very basic information.

  • Ambush: they try to catch lone adventurers or careless stragglers with trapdoors, nets, tripwires, and the like, and hustle the captive away before help comes. Captives are robbed, stripped, tied up, and beaten, and later returned helpless to the main corridor, at the mercy of wandering monsters.
  • Fighting: a nasty bite for 1-3 hit points. They have copied their jermlaine cousins’ trick of beating captives with loaded clubs to stun them, and a victim caught by their traps is almost certain (90%) to be treated this way.
  • Tunnels: the entrances are hidden and found only as secret doors are. The tunnels are small and hard for anyone of human build to get into.

The necrophidius looks like the skeleton of a giant snake with a fanged human skull for a head. It is not undead, despite several features suggesting otherwise; a cleric cannot turn it, for example. It is made for one specific purpose, so it is usually met as an assassin or guard, never as a wandering monster.

  • Nature: completely silent; immune to sleep, charm, and mind-affecting spells, and to poison; never needs to check morale.
  • Bite: 1-8 hit points, and paralysis for 1-4 turns unless the victim saves against magic (it is not venom).
  • Surprise: 50% of the time (1-3 on d6).
  • Dance of Death: if not itself surprised, it performs a hypnotic, semi-magical swaying that holds the attention of anyone watching who fails a save against magic. Those who fail cannot act (treat as hypnotism), letting the worm advance and attack unopposed.

Making one: there are three ways:

  1. a special magical tome, like a manual of golems;
  2. a high-level magic-user using limited wish, geas, and charm person;
  3. a high-level cleric using quest, neutralise poison, prayer, silence, and snake charm.

The materials are the complete jointed skeleton of a giant snake (poisonous or constrictor) and the skull of a cold-blooded murderer killed within the previous 24 hours. It costs 500 gold pieces per hit point and takes 10 days to make.

The needleman is an intelligent plant that lives in woods. It looks like a zombie but is neither animal nor undead. Its “flesh” is covered with masses of small, sharp needles, like pine needles. Needlemen seem to hate elves and attack them on sight.

  • Needles: each round it can “fire” 1-6 needles, each doing 1-2 hit points, to a range of 20’ with the accuracy of an arrow at short range. Its supply is, for practical purposes, endless.
  • Magic: it is especially vulnerable. Magical attacks do triple damage (it still gets its normal saving throw), and non-damaging spells such as charm plants are triply effective where that applies. Being a plant, of course, it is immune to certain spells.
  • Camouflage: among conifers or heavy undergrowth it is nearly (75%) undetectable and surprises 75% of the time. It is very rarely met outside such surroundings.

A nilbog looks exactly like a normal goblin and has all the traits of that race (see the MM, Goblin), with one important exception: it suffers from a strange reversal of space and time. Why only goblins are prone to this disorder is a mystery; no other creature is known to have had it. Nilbogism (as it is called) seems to arise when very heavy use of magic strains the fabric of space and time, causing very strange local events. The combination of conditions that causes it is extremely rare and only partly understood. The nilbog does not pass the disorder on to those around it, but some of its effects are passed on.

  • Reversed behaviour: accounts of the disturbances near nilbogs vary widely, but all agree that adventurers lose control of their own actions and generally do the opposite of what they intend. They may, for example, feel an overwhelming urge to load all their treasure into an empty chest in the nilbog’s lair and leave empty-handed. There is no saving throw and no known defence (though a powerful spell such as wish, properly used, has a good chance of giving local immunity).
  • Reversed damage: when struck, it gains hit points equal to the damage rolled. It loses hit points only through things like cure wounds spells cast on it or healing potions forced down it.

Encounters with nilbogs are dreaded, so normal goblins tend to be treated with great caution in case they are nilbogs. There seems to be no way to tell the two apart except by spells such as commune, or by trial and error.

At first sight the nonafel looks like a large black panther with yellow, bloodshot eyes. It usually lives in caves in warm parts of the underworld and eats meat. Its skin has fetched as much as 1,500 gold pieces.

Splitting: it has a most unusual power to divide into nine separate black panthers, taking one segment and apparently by instinct, with no concentration by the “parent”.

  • It always attacks adventurers or any other monster it meets. Usually (90%) it splits as soon as it sees its enemies and the nine “children” try to surround them, working together as if linked telepathically into one shared mind. Only rarely (10%) does it stay whole when it attacks, and even then it splits after 1-2 melee rounds of combat.
  • Hit points: the parent has 9 hit dice and each child 1 die. When it splits, the parent’s hit points are divided as evenly as possible (a 49-hit-point parent becomes five children of 5 hit points and four of 6).
  • Attacks: the parent attacks as a 9HD monster, swinging its flail-like tail over its head like a wyvern for 2-20 hit points. Each child fights as a 2HD monster, using its tail the same way for 1-8 hit points.

Rejoining and healing:

  • If one or more children are damaged, there is a 25% chance each melee round (not cumulative) that they rejoin into the parent, by blinking together. All must be within a 50’ radius, or it does not happen. They can still fight in the round they rejoin.
  • Rejoined, the parent regenerates 9 hit points per round, one for each child. Any share belonging to a child that was not hurt is lost, not passed to a damaged one.
  • After one round of regeneration, the parent splits again into nine (or fewer, if some have died); it can fight in the round it splits. Then the whole process starts again, with a 25% chance each round of rejoining if any child is damaged.
  • A killed child’s body blinks back to the parent when they rejoin, but regeneration does not help it, so there is one fewer child at the next split.
system.hpNote: When it splits, its hit points are shared as equally as possible among the nine 1-die children (FF p.68).

system.description: Norkers are distant relatives of hobgoblins and look much like them, but have grown 3” fangs with which they bite for 1-3 hit points in melee. In the same round they can also hit the same opponent with a club for 1-6. If disarmed they have no effective claw attack. Their very tough skin, a kind of exoskeleton, gives them armour class 3. In all other ways they are like hobgoblins (see the MM).

Nycadaemons are among the most powerful natives of the Middle Lower Planes. Like their cousins the mezzodaemons, they are common in Tarterus, Hades, and Gehenna, but unlike them they can also enter the 666 Layers of the Abyss and the 9 Hells as they please. All lesser creatures avoid them: night hags, mezzodaemons, lesser and greater devils, and most demons (see the MM). The race is utterly wicked and domineering, caring nothing for whom or what they enslave or exploit, but always acting intelligently and carefully to maximise their own power and safety, so they will work with other evil beings whenever it benefits them.

  • Strength: they are about as strong as stone giants (see the MM) and get +8 on damage, so their huge horny fists do 9-16 hit points per blow. They use suitably large magic weapons with a shield (compare the mezzodaemon) whenever they can get them, and are then +4 to hit because of their strength.
  • Magic items: clever and capable, they can use all kinds of magic items suited to their size and nature. But their graded magic resistance stops low-level magic working except rarely, and makes even higher-level spell devices fail with distressing regularity, so they usually shun all but the most powerful magical objects (some miscellaneous items, artifacts, relics, and the like) and enchanted weapons with no magical effects for their many-planed nature to disrupt.
  • Powers: command (three times a day), dispel magic (twice a day), dimension door (three times a day), gaseous form (once a day), mirror image (4 images, twice a day), reverse gravity (twice a day), wind walk (three times a day), and word of recall (once a day). Also, one per round: comprehend languages, detect invisibility, detect magic, enlarge (and its reverse), fear (by touch), invisibility (up to 10’ radius), polymorph self, project image, read magic, and telepathy.
  • Defences: only weapons of +2 or better harm them; iron and silver weapons do not unless so enchanted. Paralysis and poisons (including all gases) have no effect, and acid, cold, and fire do half damage. They regenerate 3 hit points per turn (0.3 per melee round). Beguiling, charm, and suggestion never affect them.
  • Magic resistance: 100% against 1st-level magic, falling in 5% steps (compare the mezzodaemon) to 60% at 9th level. This assumes an 11th-level caster; it drops 5% per level for casters of 12th level or more and rises the same for casters of 10th level or less. Examples: against a 5th-level spell from a 13th-level magic-user, 80% − 10% = 70%; against a 4th-level spell from a 10th-level magic-user, 85% + 5% = 90%.
  • Senses: they see the whole spectrum of radiation (infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays, etc.), and can communicate telepathically with creatures of low intelligence or better.

Each nycadaemon guards its personal name most carefully, to avoid being trapped or enslaved by some demon lord, arch-devil, or the like.

system.treasure: Individuals M; in lair B, S
system.description:
The ogrillon is a smaller kind of ogre, an orc-ogre crossbreed, and behaves generally like its larger cousin (see the MM, Ogre), with one exception: it never uses a weapon, fighting with its horny fists. With its 18(01) strength, each fist does 2-7 hit points on a hit.

Most look like orcs and often travel with them for short periods; there is a 90% chance an ogrillon cannot be told from an orc, even in the same group. Some (10%) look ogrish, though smaller; these also go with orcs, but are easy to pick out. Ogrillons speak only ogrish and their alignment language.

The osquip is a hairless, rodent-like creature the size of a small dog, with many legs: usually 6, sometimes (25%) eight, and rarely (5%) ten. Its hide is a very pale, almost colourless yellow, like very supple leather. Its small eyes are set close together, each well protected by ridges of hide-covered bone. Its jaws are unusually large, the whole bony structure jutting several inches beyond the flesh, with big spade-like teeth in each.

  • Lair: in a complex of tunnels under the basements of town buildings, or in a dungeon. The tunnels are fairly extensive, and their entrances are too small for a human or other man-sized creature to pass comfortably and are carefully hidden (found only as secret doors are).
  • Fighting: it eats rats, mice, and other small vermin, but it is ferocious and always attacks without fear, sometimes bursting out of a hidden entrance to surprise a victim. Its powerful jaws bite for 2-12 hit points. Its high dexterity gives it natural armour class 9.
  • Burrowing: its jaws let it dig through rock at a ½” movement rate.
  • Neighbours: its behaviour toward other tunnel-dwellers, such as jermlaine, mites, and snyads, is unpredictable. Sometimes it works with one or more of them; at other times it raids their tunnels to hunt.

system.hd: Body variable; head and gut when detached 4
system.acText: Normal 10; head and gut when detached 8
system.move: As normal woman; head and gut when detached 12"
system.xp: Variable, but at minimum V/290 + 5 per hit point
system.description:
The pénanggalan is a fearsomely powerful, nauseating female vampire-type undead.

By day it looks like an attractive human woman, the woman it was before death, who may be of any class.

  • She fights with the abilities she had in life: spell use if she was a spell-caster, thieving abilities if a thief, and so on, using the weapon (or weapon type) she favoured. Her body takes the damage it could take in life (fully rested) and she fights at that experience level. The head, however, takes 4HD of damage, so keep its hits separately in case the head itself is struck.
  • If she was a cleric, of whatever alignment, she cannot use “good” spells now and must keep to harmful ones.
  • Know alignment shows the alignment she followed in life, but as undead she acts as lawful evil.
  • In this form she is unaffected by holy/unholy symbols and cannot be turned or dispelled. In either form, like other undead, she is immune to all spells that try to control mind or body.
  • If weaponless in human form, she can bite for 1-6 hit points, but avoids it for fear of revealing what she is.

Joining a party: in this guise she tries to befriend unwary travellers and join them. She is very useful: over her years of undeath she has learned the dungeon she haunts thoroughly, and can lead parties to treasure and warn them of dangers. Naturally she has a plausible reason for knowing, and may sometimes make “deliberate mistakes” or pretend not to know places she does, so as not to arouse suspicion (a companion who seemed to know everything would naturally be suspected). Having joined a party, she stays with it, even out of the dungeon, but she never camps with it for the night in the dungeon or spends the night with it in the supposed safety of the upper world, always finding an excuse to be elsewhere.

By night it takes its true undead form. Its head and internal organs detach from the body, rising straight up out of the abdomen, and fly off to feast on the living blood of humans. So it always returns to one of its secret lairs before nightfall (a single pénanggalan may have as many as six identical lairs hidden around the dungeon).

  • Anyone who witnesses the head and gut detaching must save against magic or die at once; one who saves is treated as if under feeblemind.
  • It particularly likes the blood of young children or pregnant women; lacking those, it picks the party member who seems most susceptible to hypnosis, preferring women to men. It always attacks humans and ignores even near-humans.

Feeding: when it finds a victim, the head tries to hypnotise him. He must save against magic at −3 or fall completely under its control for as long as it takes to feed. It makes two small cuts in his throat and drinks his blood all night.

  • Each night’s feeding costs the victim 1-6 hit points and 1 point each of strength and constitution. It picks the same victim each night if it can, and keeps coming back until he dies.
  • The victim is “asleep” throughout and never actually sees it, even if he saves; it never attacks someone awake. If a victim survives the night, he remembers nothing but snatches, like a half-remembered dream.
  • Each night it must hypnotise him again, and his save gets harder: −4 the second night, −5 the third, and so on. A break of one or more nights stops this progression, and a new attempt after a break is again at −3.
  • Lingering drain: if he somehow escapes further visits, he keeps losing 1 hit point per night until he dies or dispel evil is cast on him. The drained hit points cannot be restored by magic such as cure wounds spells (in effect his maximum hit points are being drained); such spells work on the lost points only after dispel evil, and even restoration has no effect. Lost strength and constitution likewise cannot be recovered until after dispel evil. After that, hit points return at 1 per day and strength and constitution at 1 point each per week.
  • Saving: a victim who saves against the hypnosis cannot be influenced by it any further; it flees from him in fear and seeks other prey. He is immune to further attempts by that pénanggalan and can recognise any pénanggalan for what it is, in whatever guise. He still loses 1 hit point per night, as above, if it has fed on him at least once.

The flying head:

  • Anyone who sees the detached head and gut (for example, a victim who wakes before hypnosis begins) must save against fear or flee in terror.
  • In this form it can be turned or dispelled by a cleric, as a wraith on the cleric/undead matrix. Turned, the head and gut must return to the lair and stay there that night; dispelled (a D result), they are destroyed and the body decays (see below). A strongly presented holy symbol makes them recoil, though it does not harm them.
  • When separated, the head takes 4HD of damage. In either form it takes normal damage from all weapons.
  • The detached organs constantly drip a highly volatile, foul mixture of blood and digestive juices that does 1-4 hit points to bare flesh, which breaks out painfully in sores and boils. The liquid evaporates after one round in the air.
  • It is manoeuvrability class D in aerial combat.

Its victims:

  • A man it kills stays dead. If someone tries to raise him, his chance of surviving the system shock is halved, and if it fails no further attempt can succeed.
  • A woman it kills rises from the grave after three days as a pénanggalan (not under the original’s control). A raise attempt during those three days has the same halved chance, and if it fails, nothing more can be done; her transformation is then unstoppable.
  • Any victim successfully raised returns to normal (all hit points, strength, and constitution restored) after two months of rest, and is immune to further pénanggalan attacks and can recognise one for what it is.

Weaknesses:

  • Vinegar: once the head and gut leave the body, the organs swell, whether it feeds or not, and cannot go back into the abdomen until soaked in vinegar for an hour, which shrinks them to normal. So it always keeps a large vessel of vinegar hidden in each lair, and a lair can often be found by the strong smell of vinegar.
  • Sunlight: if a ray of sunlight strikes the detached head and gut, the head is paralysed and falls helpless to the ground until nightfall, so it always tries to rejoin its body before cockcrow.
  • Time: if head and body are not rejoined within seven hours of separating, both begin to decay and the evil life force animating it is forced back to Hell. So destroying either the body or the head is a sure way to destroy the creature.
system.hpNote: The body has the hit points the woman had in life, by class and level; keep a separate count for the head (FF p.71).

system.treasure: 1-4 gems and 25% chance of 100-600 gold pieces
system.description:
A brightly coloured insect, rather like a grasshopper about 2” long, in red, yellow, ochre and light blue. It lives in the outer regions of deserts, where nomads prize it: its antennae are water-diviners, vibrating and giving off a low hum within 120’ of a large quantity of water.

It is usually harmless, but attacks in large numbers if disturbed, by accident or not.

  • Attack: it leaps on its victim and grips bare flesh with the pincers at the rear of its abdomen. A hit does 1-3 hit points of damage and drains water and other body fluids, costing the victim 1 point of constitution. The drain continues every round after that, with no further to-hit roll needed.
  • Removing it: the pincers keep their grip even after it dies, and pulling it off does a further 1-4 hit points of damage.
  • Constitution loss: a victim whose constitution falls below 3 collapses unconscious; below zero, he dies. A survivor regains lost constitution at the same rate as lost hit points. If the victim is killed, raise dead restores only half his original constitution, and raise dead fully only 75% of it.

Phantom stalkers come from the Elemental Plane of Fire. On the Prime Material Plane they are usually found only as servants of high-level magic-users, conjured by a spell similar to the one that summons an invisible stalker (see the 1e FRPG MM). They serve as bodyguards, fighting to protect their masters.

  • Orders: a wizard must word its instructions with great care. It follows orders to the letter and twists their intent where it can, eager to be sent home.
  • Vengeance: one instruction is built into the conjuration. If the summoner is killed, the stalker(s) vanish at once and reappear 1-4 hours later, bent on vengeance, having tracked the slayer unerringly from the Ethereal Plane. They gain this ethereal tracking ability only when their master dies, and lose it as soon as the slayer has been tracked down.
  • Form: they can polymorph themselves and have appeared in various forms. The commonest is a reddish humanoid 8’ tall with huge fiery eyes. They can fly in any shape, though their manoeuvrability class varies with the shape.
  • Attacks: usually two sharp claws, each doing 1-4 hit points of damage.
  • Fire and cold: fire cannot harm them, and magical fire attacks actually heal them 1 hit point per attack die. They save against cold at −2, and cold attacks do 1 extra hit point of damage per die.
  • Death fireball: if a melee is going against it and its death is near, it can release its life essence as a single 6-dice fireball, then dematerialise and die. It sometimes explodes the fireball on itself to harm as many foes as possible. This is a last resort only, and is never done if it would harm its summoner, unless the summoner is directly and immediately responsible for its death (for example, by ordering it into a hopeless, suicidal battle).

system.specialDefenses: Invisibility; silver or magic weapons to hit
system.description:
This undead creature usually stays in the room or corridor where it was originally “killed”. Its bond with that place is so strong that there it counts as a ghoul on the cleric/undead matrix. A wandering poltergeist is met only rarely, and is turned or destroyed by clerics as if it were a skeleton.

  • Defences: it is invisible (−4 to hit unless the attacker can see invisible) and non-corporeal; only silver and magical weapons can harm it.
  • Attack: it throws any nearby object light enough for a man to throw, hitting as a 5HD monster. A victim struck takes no damage, but must save against fear (spells) or flee the area, running in random directions for 2-24 melee rounds before recovering.
  • Dropping things: a fleeing victim has a 50% chance of dropping whatever he holds at some point during the flight. Roll for how many rounds he flees, then whether he drops what he holds, and if so, in which round of the flight.
  • Once a person makes his saving throw, he is immune to its fear effect for as long as he stays in that area.
  • Sprinkled holy water or a strongly presented holy symbol drives the poltergeist back, but does not harm it.

system.xp: 6HD: V/400 + 6 per hit point; 7HD: VI/575 + 8 per hit point; 8HD: VI/925 + 10 per hit point
system.description:
Protein polymorphs are intelligent colonies of cells that can take any form they choose. They are very versatile, and feed on humans and animals with little regard for type or size, so they generally take whatever form is likely to draw prey.

  • Forms: inanimate objects, or living creatures of 8 or fewer hit dice (depending on the polymorph’s own size of 6, 7 or 8 hit dice). The form may be several shapes linked by a nearly invisible cord or film of protoplasm (10% chance to detect). The cells can specialise or de-specialise at will, taking on different textures and colours, and can change completely in a single round. A polymorph might imitate a pile of treasure, a small room, a party of half a dozen humans or a dozen kobolds. It may mix real objects into its structure for authenticity (a room or corridor may be partly stone and partly polymorph), and imitated creatures may wear real clothing and wield real weapons, often taken from earlier victims.
  • Limits: it cannot copy facial expressions accurately or imitate speech convincingly, which may give away an imitation of living creatures. When disguised as an object, there is a base chance of spotting the imposture from 10’ away (the book does not give the percentage), and touching it reveals the living cells at once.
  • Attack: normally it bludgeons its prey, then enfolds and crushes it for 6-36 hit points of damage per round. When imitating weapon-wielding creatures, one or several, it attacks as those creatures would, doing damage by weapon type.
  • Abilities: it has the normal strength of the creatures it imitates, but none of their special abilities.

system.xp: Warrior II/28 + 2 per hit point; Leader II/50 + 3 per hit point
system.description:
Little is known of these great, white, shaggy bipeds. Some say they were once a warlike race of cannibals, and their aggression is not in doubt: any party that flees or threatens them is certain to be attacked, and even one that keeps still within their view is 75% likely to be attacked.

  • Weapons: 70% of groups are unarmed and fight with two claws for 1-4 hit points of damage each. The other 30% carry battle-axes or two-handed swords. A group is always either all armed or all unarmed (except its leader), never mixed.
  • Leaders: for every 12 quaggoths there is one leader-type with 15 hit points, 3HD and armour class 4, always armed with a battle-axe or two-handed sword.
  • Poison: totally immune.
  • Berserk: a quaggoth reduced to between zero and −5 hit points keeps fighting berserk at +2 to hit and +2 damage. At −6 hit points it dies.
  • Elves: they especially hate surface-dwelling elves, and have been known to become slaves of the drow to help them in their wars against elves.
  • Speech: a halting, primitive form of the common tongue; they can grasp only very simple ideas.

Quippers are small, vicious, dark green fish of a rare cold-water piranha species. They usually swim in large shoals in freshwater lakes and streams.

  • Whether they attack: if someone swims or wades near a shoal, there is a 25% chance the quippers do not attack.
  • First round: if they do attack, roll percentage dice again for the percentage of the shoal that tries to hit in the first round, and roll attacks for that many. A hit draws blood with their sharp teeth and does 1-2 hit points of damage.
  • Frenzy: if at least one hits, the whole shoal goes berserk and attacks in the next round, making double the normal number of attacks per round. No more than 20 can attack a human-sized victim at once.
  • Misses: if every quipper attacking in the first round misses, they are only 40% likely to keep attacking the next round.

system.treasure: Most types in lair but in small quantity (10% of A at most)
system.description:
Qullans are large, strong, seemingly insane humanoids. They wear warpaint in a wild mix of clashing colours and proudly show off their battle scars, often highlighting them with paint. They never wear armour, going naked or in tiger skins. They have never been befriended by humans or near-humans: in every encounter so far they have attacked, whatever the party’s alignment or size.

  • Swords: they fight with broadswords honed to an incredible sharpness by a technique no man has copied. The swords are +3 to hit and +3 damage (5-11 damage), but blunt easily: each hit has a cumulative 20% chance of blunting the sword back to an ordinary broadsword. They wield them two-handed, though this gives no advantage.
  • Confusion: every qullan constantly radiates confusion in a 5’ radius. Anyone in melee with one must save or be confused. Roll d6 each round until the victim saves: 1-2 stands still; 3-4 attacks the nearest qullan with no thought for safety; 5-6 attacks the nearest friend. The victim may try to save each round he is within the radius, and the effect ends if he moves out of it.
  • Total chaos: forcing a qullan to do anything it would not normally do makes its confusion power “feed back” and kill it instantly. The same happens whenever it fails a save against any charm or control type of spell. So no one has learned how they forge their edges, or persuaded one to re-sharpen a sword for a non-qullan.
  • Captured swords: a human or near-human may use a qullan sword, since it is not magical, but it still has the normal chance of blunting on each hit, so it keeps its special qualities for 5 hits at most.

Demogorgon builds retrievers in his laboratories in the Abyss (see the 1e FRPG MM, Demon, Demogorgon), deliberately designing them to strike the greatest possible terror. They are rarely found on the Prime Material Plane except on a mission to retrieve (usually dead or alive) someone who has offended Demogorgon or another of the more powerful beings of the Abyss. Demons sometimes mount howdahs on their backs and ride them to the hunt.

A retriever is a giant spider-like creature, about the size of a mammoth, whose front four limbs end in huge cleavers. Despite its size it is very fast and nimble in the open, where it has room to manoeuvre.

  • Eye rays: it has six eyes, two for seeing and four that project rays: fire, cold, lightning and transmutation. Up to 2 rays can be used each round (determine which at random). Each ray hits one target within 60˝, and an eye that has been used cannot be used again for 6 rounds while it recharges.
  • Fire, cold and lightning each do damage equal to the retriever’s current hit points; a save against dragon breath halves it. If the owner fails to save, his magic items must also save.
  • Transmutation turns the victim into mud, stone, gold or lead (determine at random); a save against petrifaction means no effect. Stone to flesh restores someone turned to stone, but only a philosopher’s stone can restore a lead or gold figure. Someone turned to mud can be revived only by mud to rock followed by stone to flesh, both cast within one turn of the transmutation.
  • Cleavers: it can strike one victim with all four at once, each doing 3-18 hit points of damage, but cannot use its eye rays in the same attack. Generally it uses its rays first, then its cleavers while the eyes recharge.
  • Terror: lesser creatures flee in panic on seeing one. Even an adventurer of 5th level or lower (or a monster of under 6 hit dice) flees when a retriever comes within 30’, unless he saves against magic.

In exceptional cases, someone who died a violent death returns from beyond the grave as a revenant to take vengeance on the killer. Few can make this journey: the character must have had wisdom or intelligence above 16, a constitution of 18, and all characteristics totalling 90 or more. If both conditions are met, there is a 5% chance of returning as a revenant.

Purpose: it exists only to take vengeance on its killer, and on anyone who helped in the killing. It never attacks anyone else except in self-defence, but stops at nothing to reach its goal, and can locate its prime victim wherever he is. It tracks helpers only if they are still with the killer; if they are elsewhere, it ignores them and concentrates on the killer. Helpers who are with the killer are dealt with after him, counting as “killers” too, and they cannot escape: if they flee while it is busy with the killer, it tracks every one of them down afterward. When it has killed all its intended victims, it immediately crumbles away and never returns; its spirit rests in peace.

  • Not evil: although undead, it is driven by sheer will, not evil, so clerics cannot turn or destroy it, and holy/unholy symbols, holy water and other religious items do not affect it. Like other undead it is immune to all spells that try to control or influence mind or body; otherwise it keeps the magic resistance it had in life.
  • Hard to kill: no weapon, normal or magical, affects it, and the surest way to destroy it is to burn it to ashes. Even dismembered, its limbs keep working as if guided by one mind, and like a troll (see the 1e FRPG MM) they slither together and rejoin. It regenerates 3 hit points per round even after “death”, unless burned. It is immune to acid and gas.
  • Time limit: the body it inhabits decays only a little more slowly than normal. After 3-6 months it decomposes rapidly and the spirit must return to the plane it came from.
  • Strangling: it locks its claw-like hands around the victim’s throat and strangles him for 2-16 hit points of damage per round, not letting go until he or it is dead. If needed it uses other methods, with great cunning and guile, but never under any circumstances uses weapons.
  • Stare: it can stare into its killer’s eyes; the killer must save against magic or be paralysed with terror for 2-8 rounds. This works on no one but the killer.
  • Abilities: it keeps all the abilities it had in life, but has 8 hit dice whatever its former level, and is always neutral, whatever its alignment in life. It speaks the neutral and common tongues fluently, but its stiff vocal chords keep it from speaking except in extreme need (for example, to cast a spell at its killer if it was a spell-caster). It may never cast a spell of any kind at anyone but its killer.
  • Appearance: pale and corpse-like, with pallid skin stretched tight over hollow cheekbones, and unusually cold, clammy flesh. Its sunken eyes are sometimes dull and heavy-lidded, but blaze with unnatural intensity, especially as it nears its victim. Animals shy away from it, and it carries an unmistakable air of tragic anger, sadness and determination.
  • A new body: if the character died a particularly violent death, the revenant may be unable to return to its old body and instead takes over any available, freshly dead corpse, possibly of the opposite sex. The killer and his active associates still “see” it in its former body; others not involved in the killing see it as it is.

Rothé are small ox-like creatures with a mass of long black hair. They attack with two horns (1-3 hit points of damage each) and a bite (1-8 hit points of damage).

They are shy and dislike bright light. They generally make their lairs underground, near a lake or river with a good supply of lichen and moss to eat.

The name says it all: a man-like biped made entirely of sand, held together by some kind of magical cohesion. Sandmen clearly come from another plane, but no one knows what they are doing on the Prime Material Plane. They automatically attack humans and never need to check morale.

  • Sleep: any character or monster coming within 20’ of one must save against magic or fall asleep, whatever its level. Those who stay awake must save again each time they touch the sandman or are touched by it (hitting it with a weapon does not count as a touch).
  • Sleepers: once a victim is asleep, the sandman takes no further action against him and leaves him to doze, though in its lair it throws the sleeper out first. Sleepers stay asleep for 3 full turns whatever happens. After that, each turn there is a cumulative 10% chance a sleeper wakes on his own, and a 95% chance per round of waking if violently disturbed.
  • Missiles: sandmen naturally have protection from normal missiles.

These are enchanted versions of ordinary scarecrows, made from a variety of materials (wooden bodies and limbs, turnip heads, for instance), so their appearance varies, but they always look evil and malign.

  • Making one: it needs either a special manual, or a high-level evil cleric casting animate object, quest, prayer and command. It takes 3 weeks, but materials cost only 1 gold piece per hit point. The scarecrow obeys its creator’s simple instructions, following orders literally as long as they need no interpretation.
  • Charm: any intelligent creature that meets its gaze is charmed unless it saves against magic. Its touch has the same effect; this needs a successful to-hit roll and also does 1-6 hit points of damage.
  • Effect of the charm: it is fascination, not obedience. The victim stands gaping, rooted to the spot as if under hold person, while the scarecrow strikes at him freely again and again. If the scarecrow is killed or leaves the area, all victims recover at once.

This small creature looks like a mephit, but as far as is known it lives only on the Prime Material Plane and owes no allegiance to demons, nor (beyond sharing their alignment) to devils. It is 3’ tall, a little smaller than a mephit, with a muscular barbed tail about 2½’ long. Its leathery wings have a 5’ span and are its only means of moving; its legs and arms are too small to be of use for movement or combat. In aerial combat it is manoeuvrability class D.

  • Attack: it always attacks and never willingly breaks off a fight, striking with its cruelly barbed tail for 1-6 hit points of damage.
  • Scream: in the presence of other beings it keeps up a painful, howling scream that only its death or magical silence can stop. Conversation, even shouting, cannot be heard over it. Anyone within 60’ without well-plugged ears must save each melee round. On a failure he cannot attack or cast or control spells, though he may defend. Only one save per round is needed, however many devilkins are in range.
  • A save lasts only for that round; to act in the next round, the person must save again.
  • A spell-caster who saves may cast a spell with a verbal component that round, even though the words cannot be heard over the screaming.

This foul creature of the Lower Planes is the essence of a demon imprisoned in the form of a shadow, which it looks exactly like. As with the shadow (see MM), it goes unnoticed 90% of the time: it is only a vague shape, easily mistaken in flickering dungeon light for the shadows of dungeon features or of the adventurers themselves. It is not from the Negative Material Plane, though, so its attacks do not drain strength as a shadow’s do. It attacks normally with two claws (1-6 hit points of damage each) and a vicious bite (1-8).

Light and darkness: its odd body makes it stronger in darkness and weaker in bright light.

  • Daylight or equivalent: AC9, and it takes double damage from all attacks.
  • Torchlight: AC5, normal damage taken, and it attacks at +1 to hit.
  • Darkness or near-darkness: AC1, it attacks at +2 to hit, and takes only half damage.

Immunities and weakness: it is completely immune to fire, cold, and lightning, ordinary or magical. A light spell cast on it, however, affects it as a fireball would, whatever the lighting at the time; for example, a light spell cast by a 5th-level magic-user does 5-30 hit points of damage to it.

Wings and leap: it has small wings, normally unnoticed (only a 50% chance even if the creature itself is seen). They are too small for flight but boost its opening leap to as much as 30’. After this leap it attacks with all four claws (1-6 each) but not its bite. It always leaps to the attack if its victims have not detected it. The wings also let it half-fly, half-run at an 18˝ movement rate for one melee round in every ten, which it usually uses to begin an escape if needed.

Spell-like powers:

  • Once per day: darkness 10’ radius, and fear over a 30’ radius.
  • Once per week: a magic jar attack on a victim. A suitable receptacle must be at hand. If the victim saves, the shadow demon is stunned for 1-3 rounds.

Shadow demons are treated as “special” on the cleric/undead table. They are thought to be formed from manes (see MM, Demon, Manes (Sub-Demon)), though the high intelligence a shadow demon shows in a fight casts doubt on this theory.

A sheet ghoul is created when a sheet phantom (see below) kills a victim. It is treated as a spectre on the cleric/undead table.

  • Attacks: two claws (1-3 hit points of damage each) and filthy fangs (1-6). Its touch does not cause the paralysis a ghoul is feared for (see MM).
  • Acid jet: each round it can also squirt a fine jet of corrosive acid from its nose at the opponent it is fighting, within 10’. This hits automatically for 2-7 hit points of damage.
  • Defenses: it is affected by all attack forms except sleep, charm, and similar spells.

This greatly feared undead is a form of wraith, unusual among undead in that it looks nothing like a human. It is a near-transparent rectangle 11’ to 16’ wide, 7’ to 12’ long, and ¼” thick. It moves along ceilings and attacks by dropping onto a victim.

  • Enveloping: if it hits, it wraps its whole form tightly around the victim like a cylinder. Only one man-sized victim can be enveloped at a time. The initial attack does no damage, but the victim suffocates for 1-4 hit points of damage each round after that.
  • The victim cannot move, and can fight back only with a short weapon (such as a dagger) that was already in hand when the creature fell.
  • Hitting it hurts the victim: any damage done to the sheet phantom while it envelops someone is also taken by the victim.
  • New ghouls: if the victim dies from suffocation (or from damage his comrades unknowingly caused), the phantom merges with the body and becomes a sheet ghoul (see Sheet Ghoul).
  • Defenses: affected by all attack forms except sleep, charm, and similar spells. It is treated as a wraith on the cleric/undead table.

It has enough in common with the lurker above (see MM) to support the idea that one is some kind of undead form of the other.

system.treasure: 15% chance of 1-4 gems each, see below
system.description:
Little is known of this unusual creature’s origin or purpose. On the Prime Material Plane it is roughly man-sized and two-legged, its body covered in faint, light blue sparks. Anyone with good hearing can hear a very faint crackling even at a distance, growing louder as it approaches. It clearly does not come from the Prime Material Plane, but why it visits is unknown. Some say it is from the Negative Material Plane; others suggest an Electromagnetic Plane bordering all three Material Planes and the Elemental Plane. Its visits are rarely long, which has led to the theory that its form here is only a projection, and that its real body never leaves its home plane.

  • Attack: a successful hit discharges 10 points of electrical damage (a save against death magic halves it). Metal armour counts as AC10 against it (magical and dexterity bonuses still apply), and it gets +2 to hit against plate mail.
  • One attack only: when a shocker discharges, it collapses into fine, inert dust, so it only ever makes one successful attack. 15% of the time, 1-4 gems are found in its body, revealed once it has discharged.
  • Hitting it: only magical weapons affect it. If struck by a hand-held metal weapon, the effect is as if the shocker had attacked: the discharge runs through the metal into the attacker. It is AC10 against such attacks, but AC0 against missiles and non-metal weapons.
  • Defenses: immune to electricity, poison, and paralysis, and unaffected by mind-affecting spells (such as sleep and charm). It has 50% resistance to other magical attacks.

system.psionicText: See below Attack/Defense Modes: See below
system.xp: 10th-12th level: VII/2,550 + 14 per hit point; 13th-15th level: VIII/3,700 + 16 per hit point
system.description:
These are undead lords of 10th-15th level, once powerful fighters (with psionic abilities if they had them in life). Only magical weapons affect them, and they have 90% magic resistance. They look like a lich (see MM): skeletal figures in the rich but faded and rotting trappings of a powerful fighter.

The circlet: it is said that ages ago a powerful, evil demi-god forced them into this lich-like state, trapping each one’s soul in a golden circlet. A skeleton warrior stays on this plane only to search for and regain the circlet holding its soul. If it ever gets the circlet, it “dies” and vanishes forever, and the circlet crumbles into worthless dust.

Control: whoever has a circlet can control its skeleton warrior within 240’.

  • Taking control: the wearer must put the circlet on, see the skeleton warrior, and concentrate on controlling it. Until he does, the warrior attacks him to destroy him and take the circlet. A character who picks up a circlet without knowing what it is may not realize the skeleton warrior is tracking him. Once control is first established, it is broken only as described below.
  • Active control: the controller sees through the warrior’s “eyes” and can make it fight, search for treasure, and so on, but cannot move or cast spells himself; he is literally unable to.
  • Passive control: the warrior stays inert and the controller cannot see through its eyes, but he can move, fight, and cast spells.
  • Losing control: control ends if the warrior and controller get more than 240’ apart, or if the circlet is taken off the controller’s head. If he still has the circlet, he can regain control later. If the circlet leaves his possession, by accident or on purpose, the warrior at once drops what it is doing and moves at double speed to attack and destroy its former controller, never resting until it succeeds or control is re-established.
  • The circlet works only if no other headgear is worn; a helm, for instance, cancels its powers, though the warrior is still aware of it.

In combat: the mere sight of a skeleton warrior makes any creature below 5 hit dice flee in panic, and clerics have no chance to turn them. They usually fight with two-handed swords, though other weapons have been seen. Whatever the weapon, they attack at +3 to hit, but the weapon itself does not become magical.
system.hpNote: Skeleton warriors were fighters of 10th-15th level (FF p.79).

system.description:
Skulks were once humans with tendencies to extreme cowardice. Over the years, growing ever more resentful of “normal” humans, they developed an increasingly good camouflage ability and can now blend into any background. There is only a 10% chance of spotting a skulk that is standing still.

They live by theft and murder on the edges of civilisation, in small bands that move often and camp in deep, dark forests or underground lairs. Their habit of attacking unsuspecting victims from behind, or murdering whole sleeping families, makes them hated everywhere, and a captured skulk usually meets an unpleasant death at the hands of the community. They are rarely seen and even more rarely caught. They are so cunning that they are almost impossible to track: even a ranger has only one-fifth his normal chance (so a ranger tracking a skulk through a secret door, for example, would have only a 5% chance of following).

  • Tactics: a skulk moves quickly and quietly, freezing into stillness and near-invisibility at the first hint of danger. It likes to attack from behind at +4 to hit, doing triple damage on a hit (as a 5th-level thief).
  • Skulks never openly attack a party that looks powerful. They may set an ambush to pick off a straggler or sentry, or (better still) strike while the party sleeps, and they much prefer weak or helpless victims.
  • They are still extremely cowardly, fleeing at the slightest wound or setback with whatever treasure they can grab.
  • Languages: the common tongue and their alignment tongue. 20% also speak another language, usually a near-human one such as elvish.

system.psionicText: Defence strength 47 Attack/Defense Modes: Nil/F, G
system.description:
The blue slaad is stronger than the red, but still a fairly weak member of the slaad race, used more often to run errands and carry out missions for the masters than for anything else. It is mainly light electric blue, streaked with grey. Blue and red slaadi are fierce rivals, and neither will help the other except in the direst emergency.

  • Attacks: each claw has two scimitar-like blades, so it effectively has four claw attacks (2-12 points of damage each) as well as its bite (2-16).
  • Psionics: defensive only.
  • Powers, at will: telekinese 1,000 gold pieces weight, passwall, hold one person (normal saving throw).
  • Gate: four times per day it can try to gate in other slaadi, with a 40% chance of the gate opening. The creature that comes is a green slaad (35%), another blue slaad (50%), or a red slaad (15%).

Slaadi: general (FF)

The slaadi are great frog-like beings who live on the outer plane of Limbo, where the githzerai also live. They are shaped like large two-legged frogs, with huge heads and extremely long, sharp claws. Some of the more powerful slaadi have polymorph self and/or shape change and sometimes appear as men (see the individual descriptions). The hierarchy rises from the comparatively weak red slaad to the dreaded masters, creatures of unequalled ferocity and malice.

  • Names and summoning: every slaad has a name and can be summoned by a form of the cacodemon spell (see PHB), which affects the red, blue, and green varieties as a type IV, V, or VI demon respectively. A slaad master has a 5% chance of appearing whenever its name is spoken; if it does, it at once swallows the summoner and carries him off to Limbo.
  • Slaadi are sometimes found roaming the Prime Material Plane on missions of woe.
  • Language: all slaadi speak a common slaad language and scorn the languages of others. They all have a special telepathy that lets them understand and talk with any intelligent creature.

Slaad symbols: each slaad has a magical symbol of rank, a jewel set in its skull beneath the skin of the forehead. It is an artificial device holding the slaad’s life-force, and certain spells can remove it.

  • Control: by threatening to destroy the gem, an intelligent being can force the slaad to carry out three “requests”, if they are within its power. This is very risky: once released and given its gem back, the slaad must be rewarded very well for its work, or it turns on its would-be controller and kills him. The reward is usually human beings, whom the slaad takes back to Limbo as slaves, though very rich treasure will do.
  • The symbols have no value of their own; their worth lies in the power to control the slaad they came from. Each is unique and easily recognized by another slaad.
  • Any slaad that sees a symbol being used by anyone but its slaad owner reacts as a slaad master does to a summoning.

Removing a symbol takes one of these spells:

  • Hold, power word: stun, or mind blank: the slaad is paralysed for 1-4 melee rounds and the symbol emerges from its forehead.
  • Limited wish: wishes the symbol from the skull into the caster’s hand. The slaad gets a saving throw; on a roll of 01-65 the symbol stays put and the slaad at once attacks the caster in a berserk fury.
  • Wish or trap the soul: as limited wish, but with no saving throw.
  • Alter reality: as limited wish, but the saving throw is halved (the spell succeeds unless 01-32 is rolled).

system.damage: 2-20/3-18/3-18 or two sword attacks at 1-8 plus bonuses
system.specialDefenses: +2 or better weapon to hit; see below
system.description:
Only four of these fearsome monsters are known to exist. They are rarely seen in slaad form, since on the Prime Material Plane they always take human form, wearing no armour but carrying deadly swords of great magical power (such as swords of sharpness).

  • Attacks in human form: two sword attacks per melee round.
  • Attacks in slaad form: two claws (3-18 hit points of damage each) and a bite (2-20). A successful bite drains 1-3 experience levels unless the victim saves.
  • Powers, at will: travel the planes, astral projection, ESP, fear, darkness 15’ radius, detect invisibility, detect magic, invisibility, advanced illusion, cloudkill, wind walk, locate object, shape change (slaad/man), flame strike, weakness.
  • Gate: once per round, with a 90% chance of opening; the slaad that comes is equally likely to be red, blue, green, or grey.
  • Once per day: any symbol, power word: stun, unholy word, an 8d6 fireball, or a phantasmal killer.

Slaadi: general (FF)

The slaadi are great frog-like beings who live on the outer plane of Limbo, where the githzerai also live. They are shaped like large two-legged frogs, with huge heads and extremely long, sharp claws. Some of the more powerful slaadi have polymorph self and/or shape change and sometimes appear as men (see the individual descriptions). The hierarchy rises from the comparatively weak red slaad to the dreaded masters, creatures of unequalled ferocity and malice.

  • Names and summoning: every slaad has a name and can be summoned by a form of the cacodemon spell (see PHB), which affects the red, blue, and green varieties as a type IV, V, or VI demon respectively. A slaad master has a 5% chance of appearing whenever its name is spoken; if it does, it at once swallows the summoner and carries him off to Limbo.

  • Gate: at will, any type of slaad except Ygorl; the gate always opens.
  • Powers, at will: fear, darkness 15’ radius, blink, ESP, know alignment, dispel magic (at 32nd level), detect invisibility, detect magic, locate object, flame strike (at double power), ultravision 60’, mass charm, astral projection, symbol of insanity, death.
  • Once per day: unholy word and any power word. Also once per day he can grant another’s wish, but this takes a melee round in which he can do nothing else, so he rarely does it.
  • Other abilities: regenerates 3 hit points per melee round while alive; shape change at will; travels the planes instantly; 18(00) strength.
  • Harming him: only weapons of +3 or better damage him.

These are hard to find even for elves: 1 chance in 4 when searching, or 1 in 3 for an elf. Pesties are totally silent and very fast, surprising others 90% of the time.

  • Thieves, not fighters: they leave their tunnels and approach adventurers only to steal small treasures: gems, coins, pieces of jewellery, small weapons, and the like. They never attack and avoid physical combat whenever they can.
  • Dexterity: +3 on all saving throws against spells that can be dodged.
  • Mites: the snyad is a cousin of the mite, and the two often work together, the mite’s skill with traps complementing the pestie’s speed.
  • Language: as far as anyone can tell they have none, yet a group works well together, and they and mites seem to reach a quick understanding in their shared task.

These ghastly undead look like animated, rotting corpses with fat green worms crawling in and out of every opening in the skull. Kyuss was an evil high priest who made the first of them on the orders of an evil deity, and the “sons” have since grown considerably in number. They are treated as mummies on the cleric/undead table and, like other undead, are immune to mind-affecting spells.

  • Fear: each son is surrounded by a sphere of fear 30’ across. Anyone entering it who fails a save against magic flees in terror.
  • Regeneration: 2 hit points per round, and severed limbs regrow, as a troll’s do. This continues even after “death”, so they can only be destroyed by fire, lightning, acid, or holy water (or holy objects such as religious symbols, holy swords, etc.) applied to their wounds.
  • Attack: a two-fisted flailing for 1-8 hit points of damage. Each hit has a 25% chance of giving the victim advanced leprosy.
  • Leprosy: fatal in 1-6 months, and each month the victim permanently loses 2 points of charisma. Only a cure disease spell cures it. The disease cancels all cure wounds spells, and an infected creature heals at 10% of the normal rate.
  • Worms: each melee round, one worm jumps from a son’s head to a character in melee with it, needing a normal to-hit roll to land. It takes one melee round to burrow through the skin, during which cold steel, holy water, or a blessed object can destroy it. Otherwise it heads for the brain, taking 1-4 melee rounds; during that time remove curse or cure disease destroys it, and neutralize poison or dispel evil delays it by 1-6 full turns. If it reaches the brain, the victim becomes a son of Kyuss, and putrefaction sets in at once.

This relative of the gelatinous cube (see MM) looks exactly like a section of ordinary stone wall. It is usually 10’ square and 2½’-5’ thick.

  • Attack: its touch paralyses. The victim must save versus paralysation or be paralysed for 5-20 melee rounds, while the stunjelly tries to surround and digest him.
  • Treasure: like the gelatinous cube, it may hold treasure of various kinds. It is not transparent, only very slightly translucent: in good light treasure inside shows only as very rough outlines, and in ordinary torchlight it looks like solid wall with nothing inside.

system.description:
About the size of a large gorilla, the sussurus at first looks like a headless ape moving on all fours. In fact this 7’ beast has no external organs and nothing like a head. It “sees” and “hears” through vibrations and disturbances in the air, so it is immune to all magic that works through the normal senses, and it can detect invisible objects and beings.

Dronesong: its exoskeleton is honeycombed with small ducts through which it constantly draws in the air it feeds on. This makes its typical “dronesong”, which stops only when it dies. The sound is like a gentle wind in trees. In still air with nothing in the way it can be heard up to ¼ of a mile away, and one closed door in between will not quiet it enough to make it inaudible at that distance. Underground, it echoes around corridors and rooms, making its source hard to locate.

  • Effect on undead: the dronesong makes undead feel “at peace” and go inert, an effect called the “sleep of the dead”. Any number can be affected, but otherwise it works like a 2nd-level cleric turning undead: skeletons on 7-20, zombies on 10-20, ghouls on 13-20, shadows on 16-20, wights on 19-20, ghasts on 20; wraiths and stronger undead are not affected. While asleep, undead cannot be turned or destroyed, but they wake to defend themselves if attacked physically.
  • Surprise: in windy places it often stays still, taking in air, and is then 10% easier to surprise (15% instead of the normal 5%).
  • Attacks: it is fast, aggressive, and dangerous, fighting with the claws on its two forepaws (1-8 hit points of damage each). If either claw hits on a roll of 18 or more (or a 20 in any case), the victim is crushed onto its exoskeletal spikes for an extra 3-24 hit points of damage from this “hug”.
  • Fire: it loathes fire and at once attacks anyone carrying a torch or lantern, trying to put out the air-consuming flames.

A sussurus is believed to live over 1,000 years. It has no language as such, but communicates with others of its kind by slight, subtle changes in the dronesong. Two sussuri are only very rarely close enough to do so.
