system.description:
Far below the surface live the svirfnebli, or deep gnomes, a race related to the gnomes of the bright world. Small parties of these demi-humans roam the underworld’s mazes of small passages, always searching for gem minerals. Their realm is in an unknown region, thought to be a closely linked series of vast caverns where thousands of them labour for their king. Only males have ever been seen, and only in very deep places.

Leaders: all males are doughty fighters.

  • For every four deep gnomes there is an extra leader-type with 4+7 hit dice.
  • With more than twenty normal deep gnomes there is also a 6th-level fighter (6+9 hit dice), a burrow warden, with two 5th-level assistants (5+8 hit dice).
  • A 6th-level deep gnome is 25% likely to have illusionist abilities of 5th, 6th, or 7th level. If not an illusionist, he is 50% likely to be able to summon an earth elemental, once per day. The type of elemental is found on this table:
d20Elemental
124 hit dice earth elemental
2-616 hit dice earth elemental
7-1012 hit dice earth elemental
11-158 hit dice earth elemental
16-18xorn
19-20summoning fails
  • Innate powers: every deep gnome can use blindness, blur, and change self once per day each, and all of them radiate non-detection as the spell.
  • Armour: leather jacks sewn with rings of mithral-steel alloy, worn over fine chainmail shirts. They usually carry no shields, which would hinder them in the narrow corridors they prefer. Armour class improves by 1 for every level above 3rd: AC1 at 4th level, AC0 at 5th, and AC-1 at 6th.
  • Weapons: usually a non-magical +1 dagger and a non-magical +1 pick (a horseman’s pick for damage). Each also carries a pouch of 7-10 special darts, hand-thrown missiles about nine inches long, with a 40’ range, doing 1-3 hit points of damage. A svirfneblin can throw two darts per melee round.
  • Gas darts: a dart that strikes breaks a small glass bead of gas. A creature struck on its front must save against poison or be stunned the next round and slowed for the four rounds after.
  • Acid darts: deep gnomes above 3rd level also carry 3-6 darts of acid that eat a three-inch hole in armour in 1 round, or do an extra 2-8 hit points of damage to unprotected targets (including armour with holes, ring mail, chain mail, etc.).
  • Fighting: as fighters of the same level, but +2 to hit when throwing darts.
  • Stealth: despite their metal armour and weapons, these small, quick creatures move very quietly. They can “freeze” in place for long periods without the slightest movement, so they are 60% likely to go unseen by any observer, even a kuo-toan. Their keen hearing and smell mean they are surprised only 1 in 12, and they surprise others 90% of the time.
  • Resistance: 20% magic resistance, plus 5% for each level above 3rd. No illusion, phantasm, or hallucination can affect their minds. Because of this and their high wisdom, speed, and agility, they make all saving throws at +3, except against poison, where the bonus is +2.
  • Senses: infravision to 120’, plus limited sight into the ultraviolet. They have the normal gnomish abilities for judging direction and depth underground and detecting slopes and unsafe walls, ceilings, or floors (see PHB, Character Races).
  • Languages: outside their own domains they talk to each other by a form of racial empathy. Their own language is a dialect of gnomish that a normal gnome is 60% likely to understand. Most also speak the underworld trade language and a fair amount of kuo-toan and drow (the tongues of their hated, feared enemies, who with the mind flayers are the worst threat to any deep gnome gem-gathering party). All can talk with speaking creatures of the Elemental Plane of Earth, which are 90% unlikely to harm a svirfneblin, though the gnome may have to pay a heavy bribe in precious metal and gems to get away.
  • Escape: when pursued, svirfnebli usually dash into a secret escape tunnel sized for them. Their larger escape routes are full of covered pits and rock deadfalls. A leader is 75% likely to carry 3-12 small rock-like crystal containers, which he scatters in the path of pursuers if no escape route is close. Each is crushed when stepped on by any creature over 100 pounds and releases a cloud of poison gas about 10’ across and 15’ high. Anyone passing through must save versus poison or fall unconscious for 1-12 turns. The cloud disperses in 2 rounds.

Deep gnomes will usually help any non-enemy for a fee, and will certainly help fight drow, kuo-toans, or mind flayers if there is a reasonable chance of beating these mortal enemies. They love gems and will take great risks to get them.

Description: a svirfneblin is gnarled and very muscular, with medium brown to brownish grey skin and grey eyes. They tend to be bald.

system.intelligence: Very (within the limitations of its existence)
system.description:
This strange freak mutation is a globule of yellow jelly about 2½” across. To feed, it must drain energy (remotely, by means no one has worked out) from a carnivorous creature while that creature is itself eating. Any flesh-rending monster will do, except those from planes other than the Prime Material and undead. This odd need explains its unique behaviour.

  1. It picks an empty cave as its lair and clings to the ceiling, where it is almost impossible to spot.
  2. When a monster (preferably a powerful one) comes in, the jelly uses charm monster to persuade it telepathically to stay and attack anyone who enters. The monster must be one that normally, or at least sometimes, eats flesh; otherwise the jelly lets it pass.
  3. It then uses its other power, an advanced form of illusion, to create two illusions: one makes the charmed monster look like a much weaker beast, and the other makes illusory treasure in the cave. Observers do not see through them unless they save against magic at −7.
  4. If the charmed creature kills an intruder, the jelly drains power through it as it eats. If the charmed creature loses, the jelly tries to charm the winner to take its place.

The tabaxi, or cat-men as most humans call them, are intelligent feline humanoids living in the remote depths of tropical jungles, avoiding humans and other thinking non-humans. They live in small prides of 2-8, each roaming a large territory and rarely dealing with other prides.

  • Hunters: they are extraordinary hunters who take prey by surprise and quick ambush; two often drive an animal straight onto the claws of a third. They hide their scent with aromatic herbs, which with their natural camouflage and quick, silent movement makes them deadly opponents in the forest. Like other cats, they sometimes “play” with wounded prey until it dies.
  • Traps: very good at recognizing traps; there is only a 10% chance of trapping a cat-man, however well hidden and cleverly made the trap.
  • Weapons: they use tools when convenient, usually bone or wooden weapons, nothing more complicated than a bola or atlatl. But they have an amazing aptitude for weapons and quickly learn to use any weapon that is not complex. They generally avoid human intruders unless they see an easy chance to get weapons.
  • Attacks: unarmed, two foreclaws (1-3 hit points of damage each) and a bite (1-3).
  • Prides: 1-3 young (1 hit die; if attacked, 50% chance to fight, 50% to flee), 1-3 males, and 1-3 females. The females fight at least as well as the males.
  • Languages: their own, plus a little of the common tongue. They will not trade, considering it demeaning.

Description: tall and lithe, moving with the smooth, easy grace of cats. Their fine tawny fur is striped with black like a tiger’s. They wear no clothing. Their eyes are green-yellow with slit pupils, and their claws retract.

system.hd: 2 per tentacle+4 for the head/body for 8 total
system.description:
This creature has many names, but “tentamort” is now the most common. Its head/body is small, a rough sphere 2’ across, dark grey-green in colour.

  • Small tentacles: a number of small tentacles with rows of suckers let it cling firmly to almost any surface and move slowly across it.
  • Long tentacles: from the opposite side grow two longer (10’) and thicker (up to 5” across) tentacles. Each has 2 hit dice, attacks as a 2-hit-die monster, and acts independently. The head/body has 4 hit dice but does not attack. Killing the head/body stops both tentacles; killing one tentacle does not affect the other. With two victims in reach the tentacles attack different targets; with only one, both attack him.
  • Wrapping: either long tentacle lashes for 1-6 hit points of damage. On a natural 20, or a roll 2 or more above what is needed to hit, it wraps around the victim, pinning his arms to his sides.
  • Constrictor tentacle: once wrapped, it constricts automatically (no to-hit roll) for 1-6 hit points of damage each round until it or the victim is dead.
  • Needle tentacle: the other tentacle ends in a hollow bone needle 6” long, the colour of bone. It does not constrict. In the round after it wraps a victim, it drives the needle in, and the victim is paralysed at once unless he saves.

Feeding: through the needle it injects a saliva-like fluid, taking two melee rounds for a full dose in a man-sized victim (one round if smaller, three or four if larger). The victim’s internal organs then soften and the creature sucks them out through the needle; a man dies after two melee rounds of this (adjust as above for smaller or larger creatures).

  • If the needle tentacle is “killed” while still injecting, it lets go, and cure disease must be given within an hour or the victim dies.
  • Once the full dose is in, only stronger healing magic saves the victim from death within an hour, even if the tentacle is detached at once. Heal works, as does regenerate followed by cure wounds.
system.hpNote: Each long tentacle has its own hit points and attacks as a 2 HD monster; the head/body does not attack (FF p.86).

system.specialDefenses: Silver or magical weapons required to hit
system.treasure: Various discharged magical items, mostly useless
system.description:
The terithran is a creature of the Ethereal Plane: a short (4’ tall) biped with long, sinewy arms and an unusually large, misshapen head. On the Prime Material Plane it looks faint and shadowy (though less so than a non-corporeal monster), which gives it AC3, though its actual AC is 6. Figures in parentheses in its statistics are for the Ethereal Plane, where it is found only in its lair.

Why it comes: it has come to dislike the swirls, eddies, and warps that heavy use of magic on the Prime Material Plane causes in the Ethereal, its homeland. When it notices such disturbances, it materialises 1’-10’ from the magic-user responsible and tries to drain his power and take him back to the Ethereal Plane for punishment. Only magic-user or illusionist magic attracts it (including magic-user spells cast by a high-level ranger), not clerical or druidic magic, and only magic that is powerful enough.

  • Single spells: usually only high-level ones attract it: an 8th-level magic-user spell has a 20% chance, a 9th-level spell 30%; a 6th-level illusionist spell 10%, a 7th-level spell 20%.
  • Repeated magic: if 16 or more spell levels of magic-user spells (or 13 of illusionist spells) are used in successive melee rounds, even with no high-level spells, there is a 65% chance it is attracted. Three consecutive uses of a magic item (such as a wand of cold) give the same chance.
  • The spells need not be cast by one person; it is enough that all take effect in the same 60’ × 60’ area. If more than one person was involved, it appears halfway between them.
  • Spells used by monsters attract it in the same way and with the same chances.

Combat: it fights with two claws (2-5 hit points of damage each) but avoids plain melee where it can, preferring its powers. It is 50% magic resistant on either plane and can be hit on the Prime Material Plane only by silver or magical weapons. It can use detect magic without limit, and has these powers:

  • Stunning blast: a charge of ethereal waves acting as power word: stun on all creatures within 10’; a save against magic negates it.
  • Drain power: removes all magic ability from a magic-user (or illusionist or ranger) until the normal time to regain spells has passed, as if all his spells had been used. A successful save as against breath weapon negates it.
  • Cause serious wounds: as the clerical spell, by touch (normal attack roll needed); no saving throw. Its touch causes these wounds only in a round when it is using this power, and then the claw damage applies too.
  • Transportation: takes itself and one other person (the offending spell-user) back to the Ethereal Plane. The victim must first be grasped (if one or both claws hit, he is grasped); there is no saving throw.

Power uses: on the Prime Material Plane it has 6 power uses per day. Its main goal is to grasp the spell-user and take him away, so it always keeps one use for transportation, with a victim or, if it cannot grasp him and the fight goes badly, alone to escape. It uses the others (up to 5) to defend itself, reach its victim, and so on.

In its lair on the Ethereal Plane, its claws do 2-9 hit points of damage each, it has 16 power uses per day, and its stunning blast also does 2-7 eight-sided dice of damage.

This beast is suspected to be the larval form of some creature from the Elemental Plane of Earth or of Fire, though some think it comes from an Elemental Plane not yet defined. It is shaped like a small purple worm, 2’ across and 4’-5’ long, but is reddish-silver in colour. It lives in rock on the Prime Material Plane.

  • Burrowing: it bores through rock at 30’ per turn, leaving a red-hot tunnel about 3’ across that stays hot for two turns. In the first turn the rock glows red and does 4-14 hit points of damage to anyone touching it with bare skin; in the second turn it looks normal again but a touch does 2-7. No saving throw is allowed either way, though noticeable heat comes off the rock, especially in the first turn.
  • Charge: it opens a fight by charging, moving at 48˝ for this short burst over no more than 30’. A charge that hits does 4-32 hit points of damage from heat and impact. After that it moves at normal speed and simply touches victims for 2-12 hit points of heat damage.
  • Burning gear: whenever it hits, by charge or touch, the prominent items the victim wears or carries on the side it struck must save against normal fire or be ruined. Against a charge these saves are at −4.
  • Fire and cold: damage from a fire attack is added to its hit points for 1-4 turns. Cold attacks do double damage to it.

These stork-like birds live only in or near water. They look much like storks, but a closer look shows their feathers are metal, pure copper in fact, so a bird is worth up to 200 gold pieces. Wisps of steam usually rise from the beak, though the body gives off no noticeable heat.

  • Temperament: the “boiler bird” is harmless and attacks only in self-defence, for example if an obviously hostile party comes within 30’.
  • Boiling jet: it squirts boiling water in a cone 10’ across at its maximum range of 40’. A victim hit takes 4-32 hit points of damage (half on a successful saving throw). All targets count as AC10 against this attack.
  • Timing: it takes one melee round to suck in and heat the water, so the jet comes one round after the bird decides to use it. It can do this only three times per day; then it tries to escape by swimming away, or if it cannot, pecks for 1-6 hit points of damage.
  • Treasure: it collects only platinum pieces or other small platinum objects, usually hidden under a boulder or in a crack in a rock face near the water’s edge.

This leech is about 1’ long and looks like an inconspicuous twig. It is always found in fresh water (streams, pools, etc.).

  • Swallowing: anyone drinking water with a leech in it has a 10% chance of taking it into his mouth, unless the water is carefully filtered first.
  • Feeding: it fastens onto the soft flesh at the back of the throat and sucks blood for 1-3 hit points of damage each melee round. After ten rounds it is fully bloated and stops.
  • Choking: each round it is in the throat, the victim has a 50% chance of choking for an extra 1-4 hit points of damage. A victim who chokes in three rounds in a row dies on the third.
  • Removal: apart from any magic that may suggest itself, the only way to kill it in the throat is to push a thin, heated metal object such as a wire into the bloated leech, which bursts it with no further harm to the victim. The person trying has a 5% chance per point of his dexterity of succeeding; otherwise he burns the victim’s throat for 1-4 hit points instead.

system.xp: Male: V/275 + 6 per hit point; Female: III/125 + 4 per hit point; Larva: I/10 + 1 per hit point
system.description:
The adult tiger fly is a large wasp, almost man-sized, with a human head and four “arms”. Females are coloured like wasps; males are a uniform dull red. In aerial combat they are manoeuvrability class C.

Males:

  • Two sickle-like forelimbs strike the same opponent, even in flight, for 1-8 hit points of damage each.
  • The other two arms try to grasp the victim (normal to-hit rolls, no damage). If both hit, the sting is delivered the next melee round with no to-hit roll, doing 4-24 hit points of damage plus poison (save against poison allowed).
  • Once it has a victim, it does not let go until one of them is dead. It can sting 8 times per day.

Females:

  • They always attack with the sting, and all four arms try to grasp (a normal to-hit roll for each). If two or more hit, the victim is grasped and stung the next melee round with no to-hit roll. A female can sting up to 6 times per day.
  • The sting does 4-16 hit points of damage and paralyses the victim (saving throw allowed).
  • Eggs: once a victim is paralysed, the female lays eggs in the body. 1-3 larvae hatch in 13-24 hours, whether or not the victim has died. Until they hatch, only a very powerful spell such as heal destroys the eggs. When they hatch and burrow out, the victim dies of massive internal bleeding.

Larvae: white grubs with horned black heads and large mandibles that quickly grow to 3½’-4’ long. They attack anything that moves, including each other, biting for 2-8 hit points of damage. Each has 1-1 hit dice, AC9, and moves at 6˝. They cannot fly until they become adult tiger flies.

This three-legged hermaphrodite is 7’ tall, naked, and hairless. It is roughly human in shape, but with striking differences:

  • Heads: three, of which the outer two are featureless. The middle head has three large, deep-set eyes (two in front, above the nose as on a human, and one at the back) and ear-like organs on each side, but no mouth.
  • Arms: three. The two at the shoulders are prehensile limbs, each ending in a 6” spike, jointed so they strike to the rear as easily as to the front. The third, growing from the middle of the chest, is like a human arm, but its hand has three strong fingers.
  • Legs: three; the outer two are stumps, and the middle one has three unusually long, strong toes.
  • Mouth: in its belly below the central arm, used only for eating; it likes decayed flesh best. Above it are three 3” tentacles that writhe constantly, of unknown purpose.

Combat: it usually shies away from other creatures, but it is unpredictable and has been known to attack adventurers for no clear reason.

  • Attacking to the rear: the spikes strike at −2 to hit, because the single rear eye gives poor depth perception. Each spike does 1-4 hit points of damage.
  • Attacking to the front: the spikes strike with no penalty. If both hit the same victim, the central arm automatically grabs his neck (no to-hit roll) and strangles him for an extra 1-4 hit points of damage.
  • Illusions: if cornered with the fight going against it and no way to retreat (it moves very slowly), it projects two illusory copies of itself, controlled telepathically. They fight as it does and take no damage, and they do damage to opponents who do not see them for what they are. Treat them as phantasmal force, except that they vanish only when the tirapheg is killed or its opponents retreat out of sight.
  • Blinding flash: as it creates the illusions it can give off a split-second flash of light to hide their appearance. Everyone within 30’ stands confused for one melee round. The tirapheg and its illusions can attack in the round the illusions appear.

The trilloch is an energy being from the Negative Material Plane. It feeds on the fading life-force of dying creatures and uses its powers to hasten the deaths that release its “food”. As far as is known, it has no fixed form.

  • Detection: normal means cannot detect it, but detect magic cast within 60’ reveals its distinctive aura, and dispel magic within the same range drives it away. No other magic is known to affect it, and no way of harming it has yet been found.
  • Bloodshed: in any melee in its presence, detected or not, all attacks are +1 to hit and hits do +1 damage.
  • Influence: it can make unintelligent monsters twice as likely to attack a party they meet.
  • Hosts: it often stays with a large, powerful monster, thriving on the life-force its victims release. If this host is killed, it attaches itself to the victor and stays until driven off, or until an even more powerful creature kills its new host, and then moves to that creature.

So little is known of trillochs that they may have other powers not yet discovered.
system.hpNote: No means of harming a trilloch is known; it has no hit points (FF p.89).

system.description:
Giant trolls are hideous crossbreeds of hill giant and troll, looking like trolls in everything but size, and they are greatly feared. Their skin is red-brown and their eyes red-rimmed. (See MM for the hill giant.) They are found in nearly every climate, and have a very keen sense of smell and 90’ infravision.

  • Attacks: despite their pot bellies they are immensely strong and do terrible damage (2-16 hit points) with their favourite weapon, a large spiked club. Only rarely (10% chance) is one met without it; it then fights with two claws (2-7 each), which can strike different opponents.
  • Regeneration: as trolls, but 2 hit points per melee round, and they cannot rejoin severed limbs.
  • Catching missiles: 25% of the time, if in reach.
  • Killing one: at least 10 hit points of fire damage must be done to it. Otherwise, once it is down to a single hit point, further damage does nothing except stop it regenerating.

Trolls: general (FF)

Trolls (fully described in the MM) are horrid carnivores found in nearly every climate and feared by most creatures. Certain creatures have crossbred with them, producing fearsome sub-species of troll.

  • Inherited traits: all the sub-species can direct their different attacks at different opponents if they wish. All have inherited some of the troll’s regeneration and its great strength, and like trolls they know no fear and attack without stopping.

Troll regeneration (normal trolls):

  • It begins 3 melee rounds after the troll is damaged and repairs 3 hit points per round, including rejoining severed parts.
  • Severed parts keep fighting: a hand can claw or strangle, the head can bite, and so on.
  • Even total dismemberment does not kill a troll; its parts slither and scuttle together, rejoin, and it rises whole, ready to fight.
  • To kill a troll it must be burned or immersed in acid, and every separate piece must be treated the same way, or it re-forms whole in 3-18 melee rounds.

These ferocious ettin/troll crossbreeds have two heads and stand at least 10’ tall.

  • Attacks: two claws (1-6 hit points of damage each) and two bites (1-10 each). Both bites go at one opponent.
  • Regeneration: as trolls, but 1 hit point every melee round, and they cannot rejoin severed limbs.
  • Habits: they prefer darkness, being mostly nocturnal, and usually live in underground caverns. Their infravision is normal.
  • Surprise: like the ettin, they are surprised only 1 chance in 6.
  • Dress: they have taken up the ettin’s style of dress, moth-eaten and filthy animal skins (see MM, Ettin).

  • To kill a troll it must be burned or immersed in acid, and every separate piece must be treated the same way, or it re-forms whole in 3-18 melee rounds.

system.specialDefenses: Regeneration; impervious to cold; magical weapons to hit
system.description:
This relative of the normal troll looks much like its stronger cousin, except that its body is very cold and partly transparent. Ice trolls live in damp parts of dungeons, usually near running water. They have superior (90’) infravision and a keen sense of smell.

  • Attacks: two claws (1-8 hit points of damage each), which may strike different opponents.
  • Regeneration: as a normal troll, but 2 hit points per melee round, and only while the regenerating parts can immerse themselves in water. A severed limb can move up to 30’ in search of water and always moves toward any water in range.
  • Defenses: unaffected by cold, and hit only by magical weapons or missiles. Fire does double damage to them.

system.specialDefenses: Regeneration; invulnerable to cold; magical weapons to hit; invisibility
system.description:
This odious creature comes from perverted magical crossbreeding of trolls and invisible stalkers. The secret of making it is thought to be lost, and only thirty or so are known to exist. It is invisible; those able to see invisible things see something very like a troll, a little shorter and with blurred features. It has a keen sense of smell and superior (120’) infravision.

  • Defenses: hit only by magical weapons. Fire does full damage, but it is immune to cold.
  • Regeneration: as a troll, at the same rate (3 hit points per round).
  • Attacks: fangs and two sharp claws, against up to 3 different opponents if it wishes.
  • Fangs: 1-6 hit points of damage, and the spirit troll adds the damage done to its own hit points.
  • Claws: 1-3 hit points of damage each, taken from the victim’s hit points and also from his strength. Lost strength returns in 2-8 turns. A character whose strength reaches zero dies; at 1 or 2 he falls into a coma, waking only when (and if) his strength recovers to 3 or more.

  • To kill a troll it must be burned or immersed in acid, and every separate piece must be treated the same way, or it re-forms whole in 3-18 melee rounds.

The tween exists on the Ethereal Plane, but observers on the Prime Material Plane see it as a smoky, human-like outline. It usually takes a squat human shape but has a limited ability to change shape.

  • Fighting it: it can be attacked only by a character able to enter the Ethereal Plane, or by means such as oil of etherealness. In such a fight it uses a weapon, usually a sword.
  • Hosts: a tween almost always has a host; it is without one only briefly (after its host dies, for instance). It prefers an intelligent human or near-human, but has no special preference for player characters. After several hours it gradually takes on the general shape and look of its host, who seems to have a “shadow” nearby. It stays with its host permanently until one of them dies, and talks to him telepathically.
  • Luck for the host: it can see a few seconds into the future and can move material things short distances, so quickly that it can change a weapon’s movement in melee, making a sword hit instead of miss, for example. A creature with a tween partner rolls twice whenever a die roll is called for (to-hit rolls, saving throws, and the like) and uses the better result.
  • Bad luck for everyone else: any other creature within 50’ of the host, friend or foe, human or not, player character or not, also rolls twice, but must use the worse result.

So a character with a tween partner is something of a mixed blessing to his companions.

The umpleby is a biped about 8’ tall, weighing about 400 pounds, covered in wild, straggly hair of various shades of brown.

Behaviour: it seems rather stupid. When it meets adventurers it simply shambles along with them, neither helping nor willing to be left behind, always getting in the way and apparently unable to move quietly. It fights if attacked, but normally neither for nor against a party; if it must, it hits with its hands for 1-4 hit points of damage.

  • Treasure sense: its looks deceive. It loves treasure and can detect precious metal and gems (more than 1,000 coins and/or 50 gems) up to 100’ away, even through solid rock. It keeps a huge hoard in its lair, but never reveals where the lair is, even under threat of death (though charm monster may overcome this).
  • Loyalty: it can speak the common tongue haltingly but rarely does. Offering it food and water (it is constantly hungry and thirsty) earns its instant, total loyalty: it helps and advises its benefactor, though it still will not reveal its lair. This loyalty breaks if the benefactor fails to give it a fair share of coins or gems found through its advice. It then leaves the party and, if pursued, refuses to cooperate in any way with any party member.

Static electricity: it generates and stores large amounts of static in its body.

  • It can deliver a total of 50 hit points of damage per day, all at once or in parts, by touch. A normal to-hit roll is needed unless the victim is unsuspecting. Metal armour of any kind counts as AC10 against this (magical and dexterity bonuses still apply).
  • It controls how much it releases per touch, usually choosing 9-16 hit points.
  • When it delivers the 50th point, it falls asleep at once. Undisturbed, it recharges to 50% after one hour, 75% after at least four hours, and full charge (50 hit points) after 8 hours. Woken before a full hour, it has recharged 4-16 points; similar partial recharging applies if it is woken between one and four hours, or between four and eight hours.
  • Hair nets: it often makes nets from its own hair, kept wrapped around its waist. It can throw one 30’ with the accuracy of a short-range arrow. The hair is very tough, 50% harder to cut, break, or burn than a magical web, though there is no danger of suffocation (see PHB, Spells).
  • It uses its nets and electricity only when threatened, and is immune to electrical attacks.

system.treasure: See below for each type of urchin
system.description:
Urchins are a family of marine creatures that look like balls 3’ across, in various colours, bristling with thousands of 3’ spines. For practical purposes they have an unlimited supply of spines to shoot.

  • Spines: the more hit dice an urchin has, the more spines it can fire per melee round. They fly with the accuracy and range of a light crossbow, with a to-hit bonus equal to the number of attacks (an urchin with two attacks fires two spines a round as a +2 light crossbow). Damage, and any extra effect, depends on the type.
  • Hunting: they have innate clairvoyance, which they use to hunt, but normally do not attack humans or near-humans unless threatened or attacked.
  • Gem: a dead urchin breaks open easily, and inside is a gem whose colour and value depend on the type.
  • On land: 90% are met in salt water, but there is a 10% chance of meeting one on land, always within half a mile of salt water. On land it rolls along, surprisingly fast.

system.specialDefenses: Semi-ethereal, immune to normal weapons and missiles
system.description:
Visions are summoned beings that look like shadows, created by the misguided research of a high-level illusionist (which quickly led to his death). They cannot return to their own plane until their physical forms on the Ethereal/Prime Material Plane are destroyed, so they roam the underworld in endless frustration, attacking everything they meet.

  • Two planes: a vision exists partly on the Prime Material Plane and partly on the Ethereal. Attacked from the material plane it is AC0; attacked ethereally, AC10. On either plane, only magical or silver weapons harm it.
  • Ageing attack: it attacks by suggestion, not physically. Each round, everyone who sees a vision within 30’ rolls 3d6, adds 3, and compares the total with his intelligence. If his intelligence is higher, he has saved: that vision can no longer threaten him, and any “ageing” he suffered from it is seen to have been unreal. If he fails, he believes he has aged ten years (see DMG for the effects of ageing).
  • Killing it: a character who kills a vision must make a normal saving throw against magic. If he succeeds, the apparent ageing vanishes; if not, it is real and permanent.
  • Spells: the clerical bless spell does 3-18 hit points of damage to it. Dispel illusion does 0-5 (d6 minus 1) per level of the caster; a 7th-level illusionist would roll d6 seven times, subtract 1 from each roll, and add the results.

These predators are close aquatic relatives of the umber hulk (see MM) and live in deep fresh water. They look like their cousins, but have only two eyes (so they lack the umber hulk’s confusion ability), slimy green skin, and webbed claws.

  • Prey and territory: they hunt large freshwater creatures but consider humans special delicacies. They are extremely territorial and fiercely defend the area around their lairs.
  • Boats: their powerful claws can rip open the hull of any passing boat, and their strength and bulk let them overturn smaller vessels.
  • Attacks: two claws (3-12 hit points of damage each) and mandibles (1-10).
  • Eels: once per day a vodyanoi can summon 1-20 electric eels to help it, with a 50% chance of success.

A saltwater species, twice as large and much fiercer than either the vodyanoi or the umber hulk, is thought to exist, but little firm information is available.

This odd but dangerous little creature looks like a nearly round bundle of bristly grey hair with two bulging eyes, two small curved horns, and a 3’ tail. It floats as if levitating, but can move about freely; in aerial combat it is manoeuvrability class D. Volts are bad-tempered and usually attack even if not attacked or threatened.

  • Bite: it first launches itself at the victim’s neck and bites for 1-4 hit points of damage. A successful bite locks it onto the neck, and it cannot be pulled off until it or the victim is dead.
  • Once attached: each round it drains blood for 1-4 hit points of damage and lashes the victim with its tail, which gives an electric jolt for another 2-12 hit points. Neither attack needs a to-hit roll while it is attached.

The vortex looks like a whirlwind 4˝ high, 1˝ across at the base and 3˝ across at the top (larger ones are thought to exist on the Elemental Plane of Air). It seems to have a will of its own and cannot be summoned. Its physical body is a small sphere about the size of a grapefruit that bobs and dodges in the middle of the whirlwind; its small size and speed make it hard to hit, which is why its AC is so good.

  • Attack: a character it “hits” takes no immediate damage but is caught in the whirling cone of air and starts to spin. He can be freed only by killing the vortex, and takes 1-3 hit points of damage per round from spinning.
  • Deadly currents: each melee round there is a cumulative 5% chance that a spinning victim is killed by an especially violent air current.
  • Capacity: one vortex can hold only one human-sized victim, or two smaller creatures at once.
  • A trapped victim cannot hit the sphere; only those outside can.

This strange creature was named in the belief that it was a plant. It does behave somewhat like one (and, oddly, druid spells affecting plants affect it), but in many ways it is not plant-like at all.

  • Body: two thin, whip-like stalks with a few small leaf-like growths, up to 15’ long when fully grown (smaller ones are just as common). They join a rounded base or “body” holding a small brain and eight small legs. It can pull the root-like growths under its body out of the ground and move slowly.
  • Habits: it hates sunlight, so it is usually found underground or deep in forests. It feeds on the remains of its animal prey; having no mouth, it seems to absorb food through the stalks and pass it to the body. Why it must root in the earth is not fully understood: it seems to survive indefinitely in rocky places with almost no soil, and a small crack in a rock seems enough for its occasional need to root.
  • Attacks: it attacks anything that moves within reach of its stalks. Each stalk hits as a 3-hit-die monster and does 1-10 hit points of damage, and they attack different victims if two are in reach.
  • Killing it: killing a stalk does not affect the body; the body must be destroyed to kill the creature. When the body reaches zero hit points or below, the whipweed dies, but the stalks thrash in a mad frenzy for one melee round before going still, attacking three times each, with each hit doing double damage. If both stalks are destroyed, the body tries to escape.
system.hpNote: Each stalk hits as a 3 hit dice monster; killing a stalk does not harm the base, which must be destroyed (FF p.94).

system.description:
This bizarre relative of the skunk has little fur, and what there is grows in dirty patches over blotchy yellow skin covered in tiny purple spots. It lives mostly in dank, filthy places where it can find carrion, its food.

  • Attacks: two claws (1-6 hit points of damage each).
  • Stench: its spots constantly give off a powerful, nauseating odour. Everyone within 30’ must save against poison or be nauseated, retching uncontrollably. Those who fail are helpless and cannot defend against its attacks. The effect wears off once the skunk beast is more than 30’ away.

system.xp: 3HD: III/90 + 3 per hit point; 4HD: III/125 + 4 per hit point; 5HD: IV/165 + 5 per hit point; 6HD: V/275 + 6 per hit point
system.description:
This weed is usually found among ruined masonry, across doors, or smothering a long-forgotten treasure chest in the underworld. It is typically extensive: an average specimen covers about 20’ square, specimens up to twice that size are known, and even larger ones are possible in theory. An average one has 3 hit dice; larger ones have 4, 5, or even 6.

  • Toxic smoke: the weed is dry and burns easily, but its smoke is toxic: anyone breathing it must save against poison or die instantly. It burns and pours out smoke for 1 round per square foot of weed. Only a strong wind blows the heavy, oily smoke away; otherwise it forms a cloud with a volume 9 times the weed’s area, which takes at least four hours to clear.
  • Fronds: it attacks with many evenly spaced fronds, 13-24 on an average specimen, placed so that at least one can attack each person facing it.
  • Dexterity drain: each frond hit drains 1-4 dexterity points (half, if the victim saves against poison). A victim who loses the full 4 points from one hit also has a nervous seizure: total collapse for 2 melee rounds, then 5 more rounds attacking at −2 to hit and moving at 75% of normal speed. Dexterity bonuses, if any, do not apply during these 7 rounds.
  • Effects of the drain: a victim whose dexterity falls below 3 is incapacitated; at zero or below he dies. A surviving victim recovers half the lost points naturally at 1 point per day; the rest return only through cure disease.

Xill are flame-red, two-legged creatures with short, powerful bodies and four arms, all of which can wield weapons at once. Their high dexterity explains their good armour class (natural AC 4) and gives them +3 to hit (+5 with missiles). Unarmed, they fight with four claws for 1-4 hit points of damage each.

Purpose: a xill seems to have only one aim in life: to reproduce. Xill are sexless and lay eggs that must feed in the stomach of a living human or near-human before hatching, so they try to take victims alive. Protection from evil always keeps a xill away, on either plane.

  • Etherealness: they can become ethereal at will. Moving from the Ethereal to the Prime Material Plane takes one segment (6 seconds); the reverse takes two melee rounds.
  • Ambush: a xill usually attacks by suddenly emerging from the Ethereal Plane near its chosen victim, surprising him 90% of the time.
  • Grapple and subdue: it uses two arms to try to grapple and the other two (perhaps holding weapons) to subdue. Subduing works like subduing a dragon: once intent to subdue is announced, all damage from the two subduing arms counts as non-lethal bruising. Each melee round, divide the total subdual damage scored by the victim’s total hit points and express it as a percentage; that is the chance the victim is subdued that round. Roll percentile dice; a roll at or under that percentage means he is subdued.
  • Grappling attacks are normal, but both grappling arms must hit, or the victim is assumed to have avoided the grapple. If the victim was subdued the round before, the grapple always succeeds.
  • Paralysis: in the round after a successful grapple, the xill injects a paralysing fluid through its claws (normal saving throw). The victim has that one round to break free by “saving against strength”: roll a d20, and if the result is lower than his strength, he escapes.

Carrying off the victim: in short, the xill tries to grapple and paralyse its victim, or subdue and then grapple him. Then it turns ethereal, taking the paralysed or subdued victim with it, and carries him to its lair on the Ethereal Plane to implant the eggs. During the two rounds of the change it cannot move, its magic resistance drops to zero, and it can be hit by weapons at −3 to hit. Once the change is complete, it can be attacked only ethereally and its normal magic resistance returns.

  • In its lair: if attacked there, it first saves and protects its young and moves any egg-carrying prisoners to safety, and only then attacks the intruders.
  • Eggs: they hatch after 1-4 days in the victim’s stomach. For the next 2-8 days the larvae together do 11-20 hit points of damage to the victim each day as they grow. Then they burst out, killing him instantly, as 2-16 small xill that grow to full size in 1-4 hours.

system.xp: I/5 + 1 per hit point; Leaders: I/20 + 2 per hit point
system.description:
These small humanoids have bright blue skin and orange eyes, and usually wear loose cloth doublets. In nature they fall between goblins and kobolds, and they generally attack kobolds. They fear humans and attack a human party only if they greatly outnumber it. They delight in taking prisoners to torture or ransom (or both), and have been known to work with wererats in this. Their lairs are usually in underground caverns or deep in forests.

  • Arms: ordinary xvarts fight with small swords (2-5 hit points of damage). In every group of 20, one carries a net to entangle and hinder opponents.
  • Leaders: if 100 are met, one is a strong leader-type, 3½’ to 4½’ tall, with 8-11 hit points, attacking as a 2-hit-die monster with a hand axe, mace, flail, or morning star (damage by weapon type).
  • Spell-users: most are fighters, but a few (5% of a group) have magic use at 1st or 2nd level. One or more tribal shamans are found in a lair.
  • Languages: their own, plus fluent goblin and kobold.
  • In the lair: there is always a leader with 11 hit points and two lieutenants with 8 each, 3-30 giant rats as guards, and females and young equal to 120% and 200% of the number of males respectively. Shamans and spell-using xvarts are present in the usual proportions.
system.hpNote: Leaders attack as monsters with 2 hit dice (FF p.96).

system.description:
The yellow musk creeper is a large, light green climbing plant with leaves like ivy, dark green buds, and orchid-like flowers of bright yellow splashed with purple. Each plant has 2-12 flowers and 1-4 buds and covers an area up to 20’ square. It is usually found in soily places underground, though specimens have been found deep in thick forests. It climbs trees and rock faces equally well, and is sometimes planted on purpose to “guard” treasure.

  • Attack: when someone comes within 10’, the flowers sway hypnotically before his face. A successful “hit” means a flower has puffed musk-scented dust into his face. He must save against magic or be entranced and walk into the mass of the plant, resisting any attempt to stop him; this takes the rest of the melee round.
  • Brain drain: once he is in the heart of the plant, aerial roots attach to his skull (no to-hit roll needed) and devour his brain at 1-4 intelligence points per round. Hitting a root makes it let go, but so many roots attach at once that the drain cannot be stopped this way.
  • Killing it: the only way is to stab its bulbous root, buried 1’ below the surface. Personal belongings of earlier victims are buried near it; the creeper seems able to scrape together enough soil to cover the evidence of its past “successes”.
  • Results of the drain: if a round’s drain takes the victim’s intelligence to zero or below, he dies, a bud flowers, and a new bud appears. If it leaves him with 1 or 2 points, he at once becomes a yellow musk zombie (see Zombie, Yellow Musk).
  • Each creeper has one yellow musk zombie for every two flowers.
  • Recovery: victims neither killed nor turned into zombies regain lost intelligence at one point per day of rest. A heal spell restores all of it at once.

Yellow musk zombies are victims of the yellow musk creeper whose intelligence has been reduced to 1 or 2 points. The victim becomes mindless, his skin turns yellow, and his eyes become fixed and glazed. The draining stops, and the plant injects a seed into his skull to germinate there. He is now a zombie under the plant’s control, fighting for it and seeking new victims to drag or lure into its clutches (see Yellow Musk Creeper).

  • Abilities: it keeps the hit points, armour, weapons, and belongings it had before its “capture”, but attacks as a 2-hit-die monster. It cannot use any spells or psionic abilities it had in life and gets no dexterity or wisdom bonuses, though strength bonuses and penalties still apply.
  • Not undead: it cannot be turned, destroyed, or controlled by a cleric. Like undead, though, it is immune to all mind-affecting spells such as charm, hold, illusion, sleep, and so on.
  • New creepers: it serves the parent plant for two months, then wanders off and drops dead in some quiet corner, unless killed before then. Either way, the seedling sprouts from the rotting corpse and grows quickly (within an hour of “death”) into a new yellow musk creeper.
  • Cure: the master plant must be killed, and then neutralize poison and heal cast on the zombie, in either order, one immediately after the other. The victim returns to his former self, but needs four weeks of rest before his original characteristics are restored.
